Heterotic Moduli Stabilisation

Preprint: DESY–13-066
M. Cicoli    S. de Alwis Affiliation:  Dipartimento di Fisica ed Astronomia, Università di Bologna, Bologna, Italy. Affiliation:  INFN, Sezione di Bologna, Italy. Affiliation:  Adbus Salam ICTP, Strada Costiera 11, Trieste 34014, Italy.    A. Westphal Affiliation:  Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron DESY, Theory Group, D-22603 Hamburg, Germany Affiliation:  UCB 390 Physics Dept. University of Colorado, Boulder CO 80309, U.S.A.
Abstract: 

We perform a systematic analysis of moduli stabilisation for weakly coupled heterotic string theory compactified on internal manifolds which are smooth Calabi-Yau three-folds up to α′\alpha^{\prime} effects. We first review how to stabilise all the geometric and gauge bundle moduli in a supersymmetric way by including fractional fluxes, the requirement of a holomorphic gauge bundle, D-terms, higher order perturbative contributions to the superpotential as well as non-perturbative and threshold effects. We then show that the inclusion of α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections to the Kähler potential leads to new stable Minkowski (or de Sitter) vacua where the complex structure moduli and the dilaton are fixed supersymmetrically at leading order, while the stabilisation of the Kähler moduli at a lower scale leads to spontaneous breaking supersymmetry. The minimum lies at moderately large volumes of all the geometric moduli, at perturbative values of the string coupling and at the right phenomenological value of the GUT gauge coupling. We also provide a dynamical derivation of anisotropic compactifications with stabilised moduli which allow for perturbative gauge coupling unification around 1016​GeV10^{16}\,{\rm GeV}. The value of the gravitino mass can be anywhere between the GUT and the TeV scale depending on the stabilisation of the complex structure moduli. In general, these are fixed by turning on background fluxes, leading to a gravitino mass around the GUT scale since the heterotic three-form flux does not contain enough freedom to tune the superpotential to small values. Moreover accommodating the observed value of the cosmological constant is a challenge. Low-energy supersymmetry could instead be obtained by focusing on particular Calabi-Yau constructions where the gauge bundle is holomorphic only at a point-like sub-locus of complex structure moduli space, or situations with a small number of complex structure moduli (like orbifold models), since in these cases one may fix all the moduli without turning on any quantised background flux. However obtaining the right value of the cosmological constant is even more of a challenge in these cases. Another option would be to focus on compactifications on non-complex manifolds, since these allow for new geometric fluxes which could be used to tune the superpotential as well as the cosmological constant, even if the moduli space of these manifolds is presently only poorly understood.

1 Introduction

String theory is a candidate for a quantum theory of gravity with full unification of the forces of nature. As such it should be able to describe the patterns of the Standard Models (SMs) of particle physics and cosmology. For this description of 4D physics, string theory needs to compactify its ambient 10D space-time. The multitude of possible compactification choices together with a plethora of massless 4D ‘moduli’ fields originating from the deformation modes of the extra dimensions, leads to vacuum degeneracy and moduli problems. Recent progress in achieving moduli stabilisation points to the possibility of an exponentially large set of cosmologically distinct de Sitter (dS) solutions of string theory with positive but tiny cosmological constant, the ‘landscape’ (for reviews see [1, 2]).

These results need to be combined with string constructions of viable particle physics. One fruitful region of the string landscape for this purpose is weakly coupled heterotic string theory. Recent works on heterotic compactifications on both smooth Calabi-Yau (CY) manifolds [3] and their singular limits in moduli space, orbifolds [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], provided constructions of 4D low-energy effective field theories matching the minimal supersymmetric version of the SM (MSSM) almost perfectly. However, in contrast to the understanding achieved in type IIB string theory, heterotic CY or orbifold compactifications lack a well controlled description of moduli stabilisation, and consequently, of inflationary cosmology as well.11 1 However, for some recent attempts see e.g. [9, 10].

As weakly coupled heterotic CY compactifications lack both D-branes and a part of the three-form flux available in type IIB, historically moduli stabilisation in the heterotic context focused mostly on the moduli dependence of 4D non-perturbative contributions to the effective action from gaugino condensation [11, 12, 13]. While this produced models of partial stabilisation of the dilaton and some Kähler moduli [9, 14, 15, 16], this route generically failed at describing controlled and explicit stabilisation of the 𝒪⁡(100){\cal O}(100) complex structure moduli of a given CY. Moreover, the resulting vacua tend to yield values of the compactification radius and string coupling (given by the dilaton) at the boundary of validity of the supergravity approximation and the weak coupling regime.

The works [17, 18, 19] proposed to include the three-form flux HH to stabilise the complex structure moduli in combination with hidden sector gaugino condensation for supersymmetric dilaton stabilisation. The inclusion of fluxes in the heterotic string was originally studied by Strominger [20] who showed that, by demanding 𝒩=1\mathcal{N}=1 supersymmetry, the classical 10D equations of motion imply H=−i2(∂−∂¯)JH=-\frac{i}{2}(\partial-\bar{\partial})J where JJ is the fundamental (1,1)(1,1)-form on the internal space. Hence a non-vanishing three-form flux breaks the Kähler condition d​J=0dJ=0. Note that this is the case of (0,2)(0,2)-compactifications which allow for MSSM-like model building and the generation of worldsheet instantons, since in the non-standard embedding the Chern-Simons term gives a non-zero contribution to the three-form flux HH. However this contribution is at order α′\alpha^{\prime}, implying that the Calabi-Yau condition is preserved at tree-level and broken only at order α′\alpha^{\prime}. Moreover, in the heterotic case, due to the absence of Ramond-Ramond three-form fluxes, there is generically no freedom to tune the superpotential small enough to fix the dilaton at weak coupling. However, a sufficiently small superpotential could be obtained by considering fractional Chern-Simons invariants (such as discrete Wilson lines) [17]. Note that it is natural to take these effects into account for (0,2)(0,2)-compactifications which are the most relevant for both model building and moduli stabilisation since, as we pointed out above, they feature a non-vanishing Chern-Simons contribution to HH, regardless of the presence of fractional Chern-Simons invariants.22 2 As we shall describe in section 3.1.1, the co-exact piece of the Chern-Simons term is responsible for the breaking of the Kähler condition d​J=0dJ=0 while the generation of fractional invariants is controlled by the harmonic piece of the Chern-Simons term.

Supersymmetric vacua with all geometric moduli stabilised could be achieved by fixing the Kähler moduli via contributions from threshold corrections to the gauge kinetic function [21, 22]. However this minimum cannot be trusted since it resides in a strong coupling regime where the gauge coupling is even driven into negative values [17]. The inclusion of a single worldsheet instanton contribution can resolve this difficulty [19]. However, none of these vacua break supersymmetry, resulting in unrealistic anti-de Sitter (AdS) solutions.

In this paper, we shall present new stable Minkowski (or de Sitter) vacua where all geometric moduli are stabilised and supersymmetry is broken spontaneously along the Kähler moduli directions. Let us summarise our main results:

  • •

    We identify two small parameters, one loop-suppressed and the other volume-suppressed, which allow us to expand the scalar potential in a leading and a subleading piece. This separation of scales allows us to perform moduli stabilisation in two steps.

  • •

    The leading scalar potential is generated by D-terms, quantised background fluxes (if needed for the stabilisation of the complex structure moduli), perturbative contributions to the superpotential and gaugino condensation. This potential depends on the gauge bundle moduli, the complex structure moduli and the dilaton which are all fixed supersymmetrically at leading order.

  • •

    The subleading scalar potential depends on the Kähler moduli and it is generated by threshold corrections to the gauge kinetic function, worldsheet instantons and 𝒪⁡(α′2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}) [23], and 𝒪⁡(α′3)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 3}) [24, 25] corrections to the Kähler potential. These effects give rise to new Minkowski vacua (assuming the fine-tuning problem can be solved) which break supersymmetry spontaneously along the Kähler moduli directions. The dilaton is stabilised at a value Re⁡(S)≃2\rm{Re}(S)\simeq 2 in a way compatible with gauge coupling unification, while the compactification volume is fixed at 𝒱≃20{\cal V}\simeq 20 which is the upper limit compatible with string perturbativity. These new minima represent a heterotic version of the type IIB LARGE Volume Scenario (LVS) [26, 27].

  • •

    By focusing on CY manifolds with K3- or T4T^{4}-fibres over a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} base, we shall also show that this LVS-like moduli stabilisation mechanism allows for anisotropic constructions where the overall volume is controlled by two larger extra dimensions while the remaining four extra dimensions remain smaller. This anisotropic setup is particularly interesting phenomenologically, as it allows one to match the effective string scale to the GUT scale of gauge coupling unification [28, 29], and fits very well with the picture of intermediate 6D orbifold GUTs emerging from heterotic MSSM orbifolds [29, 30].

  • •

    The soft terms generated by gravity mediation feature universal scalar masses, A-terms and μ/B​μ\mu/B\mu-term of order the gravitino mass, m3/2=|W|​MP/2​Re​(S)​𝒱m_{3/2}=|W|M_{P}/\sqrt{2\rm{Re}(S){\cal V}}, and suppressed gaugino masses at the %-level. In turn, the value of the supersymmetry breaking scale depends on the stabilisation of the complex structure moduli:

    1. 1.

      If the complex structure moduli are fixed by turning on quantised background fluxes, due to the lack of tuning freedom in the heterotic three-form flux, |W||W| can at most be made of order |W|≃𝒪⁡(0.1−0.01)|W|\simeq\mathcal{O}(0.1-0.01) by turning on only Chern-Simons fractional fluxes. Hence the gravitino mass becomes of order MG​U​T≃1016M_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}\simeq 10^{16} GeV for Re⁡(S)≃2\rm{Re}(S)\simeq 2 and 𝒱≃20{\cal V}\simeq 20, leading to high scale supersymmetry breaking.

    2. 2.

      If the complex structure moduli are fixed without turning on quantised background fluxes, the main contribution to |W||W| can come from higher order perturbative operators or gaugino condensation. Hence |W||W| can acquire an exponentially small value, leading to low-scale supersymmetry [31, 32].

Let us discuss the stabilisation of the complex structure moduli in more detail. In a series of recent papers [33, 34, 35], it has been shown that in particular examples one could be able to fix all the complex structure moduli without the need to turn on any quantised background flux. Note that, as we explained above, if one focuses on (0,2)(0,2)-compactifications, this observation is not important for preserving the CY condition (since this is broken at order α′\alpha^{\prime} regardless of the presence of a harmonic quantised flux) but it is instead crucial to understand the order of magnitude of the superpotential which sets the gravitino mass scale once supersymmetry is broken. Following the original observation of Witten [36], the authors of [33, 34, 35] proved that, once the gauge bundle is required to satisfy the Hermitian Yang-Mills equations, the combined space of gauge bundle and complex structure moduli is not a simple direct product but acquires a ‘cross-structure’. Denoting the gauge bundle moduli as CiC_{i}, i=1,…,Ni=1,...,N, and the complex structure moduli as ZαZ_{\alpha}, α=1,…,h1,2\alpha=1,...,h^{1,2}, this observation implies that the dimensionality of the gauge bundle moduli space is actually a function of the complex structure moduli, i.e. N=N⁡(Z)N=N(Z), and viceversa the number of massless ZZ-fields actually depends on the value of the gauge bundle moduli. As a simple intuitive example, consider a case with just one gauge bundle modulus and a leading order scalar potential which looks like:

V=(∑β=1hfix1,2|Zβ|2)​|C|2.V=\left(\sum_{\beta=1}^{h^{1,2}_{\rm fix}}|Z_{\beta}|^{2}\right)|C|^{2}\,. (1)

The form of this potential implies that:

  • •

    If CC is fixed by some stabilisation mechanism (like D-terms combined with higher order CC-dependent terms in the superpotential) at ⟨C⟩≠0\langle C\rangle\neq 0, then hfix1,2h^{1,2}_{\rm fix} complex structure moduli are fixed at ⟨Zβ⟩=0\langle Z_{\beta}\rangle=0 ∀β=1,…,hfix1,2\forall\,\beta=1,...,h^{1,2}_{\rm fix}. Hence the number of ZZ-moduli left flat is given by hhol1,2=h1,2−hfix1,2h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=h^{1,2}-h^{1,2}_{\rm fix}, which is also the dimensionality of the sub-locus in complex structure moduli space for C≠0C\neq 0 where the gauge bundle is holomorphic. Hence the best case scenario is when this sub-locus is just a point, i.e. hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0.

  • •

    If the ZZ-moduli are fixed by some stabilisation mechanism (like by turning on background quantised fluxes) at values different from zero, then the gauge bundle modulus CC is fixed at ⟨C⟩=0\langle C\rangle=0.33 3 See also [37] for a mathematical discussion of this issue which basically comes to the same conclusion that gauge bundle moduli are generically absent.

However this stabilisation mechanism generically does not lead to the fixing of all complex structure moduli due to the difficulty of finding examples with hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0, i.e. with a point-like sub-locus in complex structure moduli space where the gauge bundle is holomorphic. In fact, there is so far no explicit example in the literature where hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0 can be obtained without having a singular CY even if there has been recently some progress in understanding how to resolve these singular point-like sub-loci [38]. Moreover, let us stress that even if one finds a non-singular CY example with hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0 (there is in principle no obstruction to the existence of this best case scenario), all the complex structure moduli are fixed only if C≠0C\neq 0, since for C=0C=0 the ZZ-directions would still be flat. As we pointed out above, C≠0C\neq 0 could be guaranteed by the interplay of D-terms and higher order terms in the superpotential, but in the case when the number of CC-moduli is large, one should carefully check that all of them are fixed at non-zero values (for example, one might like to have some of them to be fixed at zero in order to preserve some symmetries relevant for phenomenology like U​(1)B−LU(1)_{B-L}). Thus the requirement of a holomorphic gauge bundle generically fixes some complex structure moduli but not all of them. Note also that these solutions are not guaranteed to survive for a non-vanishing superpotential, since one would then need to solve a set of non-holomorphic equations.

Let us therefore analyse the general case where some ZZ-moduli are left flat after the requirement of a holomorphic gauge bundle, and summarise our results for their stabilisation:

  • •

    Given that promising phenomenological model building requires us to focus on the non-standard embedding where the HH-flux already gets a non-vanishing contribution from the co-exact piece of the Chern-Simons term, we consider quite natural the option to turn on also a harmonic Chern-Simons piece that could yield a fractional ZZ-dependent superpotential that lifts the remaining complex structure moduli [17].

  • •

    If H≠0H\neq 0, as in the case of (0,2)(0,2)-compactifications, both the dilaton and the warp factor could depend on the internal coordinates. For simplicity, we shall however restrict to the solutions where both of them are constant, corresponding to the case of ‘special Hermitian manifolds’ [39].

  • •

    The inclusion of quantised background fluxes cannot fix the remaining hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 complex structure moduli in a supersymmetric way with, at the same time, a vanishing flux superpotential W0W_{0}. In fact, setting the F-terms of the ZZ-moduli to zero corresponds to setting the (1,2)(1,2)-component of HH to zero, whereas setting W0=0W_{0}=0 implies a vanishing (3,0)(3,0)-component of HH. As a consequence, given that the flux is real, the entire harmonic flux HH is zero, and so the hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 ZZ-moduli are still flat.44 4 This statement is also implicit in [18]. Note that this would not be the case in type IIB where the three-form flux is complex (because of the presence of also Ramond-Ramond fluxes) [40].

  • •

    The remaining hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 ZZ-moduli can be fixed only if W0≠0W_{0}\neq 0 but this would lead to a runaway for the dilaton if W0W_{0} is not fine-tuned to exponentially small values to balance the dilaton-dependent contribution from gaugino condensation. However, due to the absence of Ramond-Ramond fluxes, the heterotic HH-flux does not contain enough freedom to tune W0W_{0} to small values, since it is used mostly to stabilise the complex structure moduli in a controlled vacuum. There are then two options:

    1. 1.

      Models with either accidentally cancelling integer flux quanta or only Chern-Simons fractional fluxes where the flux superpotential could be small enough to compete with gaugino condensation, even if this case would lead to supersymmetry breaking around the GUT scale;

    2. 2.

      Compactifications on non-Kähler manifolds which do not admit a closed holomorphic (3,0)(3,0)-form, since these cases allow for new geometric fluxes which could play a similar rôle as type IIB Ramond-Ramond fluxes, and could be used to tune W0W_{0} to small values [39, 41, 42, 43, 44]. In this case one could lower the gravitino mass to the TeV scale and have enough freedom to tune the cosmological constant. However, the moduli space of these manifolds is at present only poorly understood.

    In this paper, we shall not consider the second option given that we want to focus on cases, like ‘special Hermitian manifolds’, which represent the smallest departure from a CY due to α′\alpha^{\prime} effects.

This analysis suggests that if one is interested in deriving vacua where our Kähler moduli stabilisation mechanism leads to spontaneous supersymmetry breaking around the TeV scale, one should focus on one of the two following situations:

  1. 1.

    Models where the requirement of a holomorphic gauge bundle fixes all complex structure moduli without inducing singularities (so that the supergravity approximation is reliable), i.e. models with hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0 [33, 34, 35]. The dilaton could then be fixed in a supersymmetric way by using a double gaugino condensate while the Kähler moduli could be fixed following our LVS-like method by including worldsheet instantons, threshold and α′\alpha^{\prime} effects. This global minimum would break supersymmetry spontaneously along the Kähler moduli directions. The gravitino mass could then be around the TeV scale because of the exponential suppression from gaugino condensation.

  2. 2.

    Simple models with a very small number of complex structure moduli, like Abelian orbifolds with a few untwisted ZZ-moduli, or even non-Abelian orbifolds with no complex structure moduli at all. In fact, in this case gauge singlets could be fixed at non-zero values via D-terms induced by anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) factors and higher order terms in the superpotential [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], so resulting in cases where all the ZZ-moduli become massive by the holomorphicity of the gauge bundle. The dilaton could then be fixed by balancing gaugino condensation with the contribution from a gauge bundle modulus (i.e. a continuous Wilson line in the orbifold language) which develops a small vacuum expectation value (VEV) because it comes from RR-symmetry breaking higher order terms in the superpotential [31, 32]. A low gravitino mass could then be obtained due to this small VEV.

Let us finally note that accommodating our observed cosmological constant, which is a challenge even with fluxes and 𝒪⁡(100)\mathcal{O}(100) complex structures, is even more of a challenge in cases without quantised fluxes.

This paper is organised as follows. In Section 2 we introduce the general framework of heterotic CY compactifications [45, 46], reviewing the form of the tree-level effective action and then presenting a systematic discussion of quantum corrections from non-perturbative effects [11, 12, 13], string loops [47, 48, 49], and higher-derivative α′\alpha^{\prime}-corrections [23, 24, 25] according to their successive level of suppression by powers of the string coupling and inverse powers of the volume. Supersymmetric vacua are then discussed in Section 3, while in Section 4 we derive new global minima with spontaneous supersymmetry breaking which can even be Minkowski (or slightly de Sitter) if enough tuning freedom is available. After discussing in Section 5 the resulting pattern of moduli and soft masses generated by gravity mediation, we derive anisotropic constructions in Section 6. We finally present our conclusions in Section 7.

2 Heterotic framework

Let us focus on weakly coupled heterotic string theory compactified on a smooth CY three-fold XX. The 4D effective supergravity theory involves several moduli: h1,2​(X)h^{1,2}(X) complex structure moduli ZαZ_{\alpha}, α=1,…,h1,2​(X)\alpha=1,...,h^{1,2}(X); the dilaton SS and h1,1h^{1,1} Kähler moduli TiT_{i}, i=1,…,h1,1​(X)i=1,...,h^{1,1}(X) (besides several gauge bundle moduli).

The real part of SS is set by the 4D dilaton (see appendix A for the correct normalisation):

Re⁡(S)≡s=14​π​e−2​ϕ4=14​π​e−2​ϕ​𝒱,{\rm Re}(S)\equiv s=\frac{1}{4\pi}\,e^{-2\phi_{4}}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\,e^{-2\phi}\,{\cal V}\,, (2)

where ϕ\phi is the 10D dilaton whose VEV gives the string coupling e⟨ϕ⟩=gse^{\langle\phi\rangle}=g_{s}. The imaginary part of SS is given by the universal axion aa which is the 4D dual of B2B_{2}. On the other hand, the real part of the Kähler moduli, ti=Re⁡(Ti)t_{i}={\rm Re}(T_{i}), measures the volume of internal two-cycles in units of the string length ℓs=2​π​α′\ell_{s}=2\pi\sqrt{\alpha^{\prime}}. The imaginary part of TiT_{i} is given by the reduction of B2B_{2} along the basis (1,1)(1,1)-form D^i\hat{D}_{i} dual to the divisor DiD_{i}.

We shall focus on general non-standard embeddings with possible U⁡(1)U(1) factors in the visible sector. Hence the gauge bundle in the visible E8visE_{8}^{{\rm vis}} takes the form Vvis=Uvis​⨁κℒκV_{{\rm vis}}=U_{\rm vis}\bigoplus_{\kappa}\mathcal{L}_{\kappa} where UvisU_{{\rm vis}} is a non-Abelian bundle whereas the ℒκ\mathcal{L}_{\kappa} are line bundles. On the other hand the vector bundle in the hidden E8hidE_{8}^{{\rm hid}} involves just a non-Abelian factor Vhid=UhidV_{{\rm hid}}=U_{\rm hid}. We shall not allow line bundles in the hidden sector since, just for simplicity, we shall not consider matter fields charged under anomalous U⁡(1)U(1)s. In fact, if we want to generate a superpotential from gaugino condensation in the hidden sector in order to fix the moduli, all the anomalous U⁡(1)U(1)s have to reside in the visible sector otherwise, as we shall explain later on, the superpotential would not be gauge invariant.

2.1 Tree-level expressions

The tree-level Kähler potential takes the form:

Ktree=−ln⁡𝒱−ln⁡(S+S¯)−ln⁡(i​∫XΩ∧Ω¯),K_{\rm tree}=-\ln{\cal V}-\ln(S+\overline{S})-\ln\left({\rm i}\int_{X}\Omega\wedge\overline{\Omega}\right), (3)

where 𝒱{\cal V} is the CY volume measured in string units, while Ω\Omega is the holomorphic (3,0)(3,0)-form of XX that depends implicitly on the ZZ-moduli. The internal volume depends on the TT-moduli since it looks like:

𝒱=16​ki​j​k​ti​tj​tk=148​ki​j​k​(Ti+T¯i)​(Tj+T¯j)​(Tk+T¯k),{\cal V}=\frac{1}{6}\,k_{ijk}t_{i}t_{j}t_{k}=\frac{1}{48}\,k_{ijk}\left(T_{i}+\overline{T}_{i}\right)\left(T_{j}+\overline{T}_{j}\right)\left(T_{k}+\overline{T}_{k}\right), (4)

where ki​j​k=∫XD^i∧D^j∧D^kk_{ijk}=\int_{X}\hat{D}_{i}\wedge\hat{D}_{j}\wedge\hat{D}_{k} are the triple intersection numbers of XX.

The tree-level holomorphic gauge kinetic function for both the visible and hidden sector is given by the dilaton:

ftree=S⇒Re⁡(ftree)≡g4−2=s.f_{\rm tree}=S\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad{\rm Re}(f_{\rm tree})\equiv g^{-2}_{\scriptscriptstyle 4}=s\,. (5)

The tree-level superpotential is generated by the three-form flux HH and it reads:

Wflux=∫XH∧Ω,W_{\rm flux}=\int_{X}H\wedge\Omega\,, (6)

with the correct definition of HH including α′\alpha^{\prime} effects:

H=d​B2−α′4​[CS⁡(A)−CS⁡(ω)],H=dB_{2}-\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{4}\left[{\rm CS}(A)-{\rm CS}(\omega)\right], (7)

where CS⁡(A){\rm CS}(A) is the Chern-Simons three-form for the gauge connection AA:

CS⁡(A)=Tr⁡(A∧d​A+23​A∧A∧A),{\rm CS}(A)={\rm Tr}\left(A\wedge dA+\frac{2}{3}\,A\wedge A\wedge A\right), (8)

and CS⁡(ω){\rm CS}(\omega) is the gravitational equivalent for the spin connection ω\omega.

The VEV of the tree-level superpotential, W0W_{0}, is of crucial importance. Due to the difference with type IIB where one has two three-form fluxes, which can give rise to cancellations among themselves leading to small values of W0W_{0}, in the heterotic case W0W_{0} is generically of order unity. Hence one experiences two problems:

  1. 1.

    Contrary to type IIB, the heterotic dilaton is not fixed by the flux superpotential, resulting in a supergravity theory which is not of no-scale type. More precisely, the F-term scalar potential:

    VF=eK​(KI​J¯​DI​W​DJ¯​W¯−3​|W|2),V_{F}=e^{K}\left(K^{I\bar{J}}D_{I}WD_{\bar{J}}\bar{W}-3|W|^{2}\right), (9)

    derived from (3) and (6) simplifies to:

    VF\displaystyle V_{F} =\displaystyle= eK​[∑ZKα​β¯​Dα​W​Dβ¯​W¯+(KS​S¯​KS​KS¯+∑TKi​j¯​Ki​Kj¯−3)​|W|2]\displaystyle e^{K}\left[\sum_{Z}K^{\alpha\bar{\beta}}D_{\alpha}WD_{\bar{\beta}}\bar{W}+\left(K^{S\bar{S}}K_{S}K_{\bar{S}}+\sum_{T}K^{i\bar{j}}K_{i}K_{\bar{j}}-3\right)|W|^{2}\right] (10)
    =eK​(∑ZKα​β¯​Dα​W​Dβ¯​W¯+|W|2),\displaystyle=e^{K}\left(\sum_{Z}K^{\alpha\bar{\beta}}D_{\alpha}WD_{\bar{\beta}}\bar{W}+|W|^{2}\right),

    since KS​S¯​KS​KS¯=1K^{S\bar{S}}K_{S}K_{\bar{S}}=1 and ∑TKi​j¯​Ki​Kj¯−3=0\sum_{T}K^{i\bar{j}}K_{i}K_{\bar{j}}-3=0. Setting Dα​W=0D_{\alpha}W=0 ∀α=1,…,h1,2​(X)\forall\alpha=1,...,h^{1,2}(X), the scalar potential (10) reduces to:

    VF=eK​|W0|2=|W0|22​s​𝒱,V_{F}=e^{K}|W_{0}|^{2}=\frac{|W_{0}|^{2}}{2s{\cal V}}\,, (11)

    yielding a run-away for both ss and 𝒱{\cal V} if |W0|≠0|W_{0}|\neq 0. Given that generically |W0|≃𝒪⁡(1)|W_{0}|\simeq\mathcal{O}(1), it is very hard to balance this tree-level run-away against SS-dependent non-perturbative effects which are exponentially suppressed in SS. One could try to do it by considering small values of s=g4​D−2s=g^{-2}_{\scriptscriptstyle 4D} but this would involve a strong coupling limit where control over moduli stabilisation is lost. A possible way to lower |W0||W_{0}| was proposed in [17] where the authors derived the topological conditions to have fractional Chern-Simons invariants.

  2. 2.

    If |W0|≠0|W_{0}|\neq 0, even if it is fractional, one cannot obtain low-energy supersymmetry. In fact, the gravitino mass is given by m3/2=eK/2​|W0|​MPm_{3/2}=e^{K/2}|W_{0}|M_{P}, and so the invariant quantity eK/2​|W0|=|W0|/(2​s​𝒱)e^{K/2}|W_{0}|=|W_{0}|/(\sqrt{2s{\cal V}}) has to be of order 10−1510^{-15} to have TeV-scale supersymmetry. As we have seen, the 4D gauge coupling is given by αG​U​T−1=gs−2​𝒱\alpha_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}^{-1}=g_{s}^{-2}{\cal V}, and so a huge value of the internal volume would lead to a hyper-weak GUT coupling. Note that a very large value of 𝒱{\cal V} cannot be compensated by a very small value of gs−2g^{-2}_{s} since we do not want to violate string perturbation theory.

Let us briefly mention that in some particular cases one could have an accidental cancellation among the flux quanta which yields a small |W0||W_{0}| as suggested in [18]. We stress that in the heterotic case, contrary to type IIB, this cancellation is highly non-generic, and so it is not very appealing to rely on it to lower |W0||W_{0}|. Hence it would seem that the most promising way to get low-energy supersymmetry is to consider the case where |W0|=0|W_{0}|=0 and generate an exponentially small superpotential only at sub-leading non-perturbative level. This case was considered in [34], where the authors argued that, at tree-level, one can in principle obtain a Minkowski supersymmetric vacuum with all complex structure moduli stabilised and 2​(h1,1+1)2(h^{1,1}+1) flat directions corresponding to the dilaton and the Kähler moduli. As explained in Section 1, this corresponds to the best case scenario where the gauge bundle is holomorphic only at a non-singular point-like sub-locus in complex structure moduli space.

If instead one focuses on the more general case where hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 ZZ-moduli are left flat after imposing the requirement of a holomorphic gauge bundle, as we shall show in section 3, the conditions DZα​Wflux=0D_{Z^{\alpha}}W_{\rm flux}=0 ∀α=1,…,hhol1,2\forall\alpha=1,...,h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} and |W0|=0|W_{0}|=0 imply that no quantised HH flux is turned on, resulting in the impossibility to stabilise the remaining ZZ-moduli. This result implies that it is impossible to stabilise the remaining complex structure moduli and the dilaton in two steps with a ZZ-moduli stabilisation at tree-level and a dilaton stabilisation at sub-leading non-perturbative level. In this case there are two possible way-outs:

  1. 1.

    Focus on the case DZα​W=0D_{Z^{\alpha}}W=0 ∀α=1,…,hhol1,2\forall\alpha=1,...,h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} and |W0|≠0|W_{0}|\neq 0 so that HH can be non-trivial. In this case one has however a dilaton run-away, implying that no moduli can be fixed at tree-level. One needs therefore to add SS-dependent non-perturbative effects which have to be balanced against the tree-level superpotential to lift the run-away. A small |W0||W_{0}| could be obtained either considering fractional Chern-Simons invariants or advocating accidental cancellations among the flux quanta.

  2. 2.

    Focus on the case with trivial HH so that no scalar potential is generated at tree-level. The dilaton and the complex structure moduli could then be fixed at non-perturbative level via a race-track superpotential generating an exponentially small WW which could lead to low-energy supersymmetry. Note that even though d​H=R∧R−F∧F≠0dH=R\wedge R-F\wedge F\neq 0 for (0,2)(0,2)-models, it is still possible to have |W0|=0|W_{0}|=0 since only the harmonic part of the HH-flux contributes to this superpotential (see discussion in section 3.1). Hence, moduli stabilisation would have to proceed via a racetrack mechanism involving at least two condensing gauge groups with all moduli appearing in the gauge kinetic functions and/or the prefactors of the non-perturbative terms. Since this is generically not the case for heterotic compactifications, this avenue will not lead to supersymmetric moduli stabilisation except perhaps for a few specific cases. Note that in this case to get a Minkowski supersymmetric vacuum one would have to fine-tune the prefactors of the two (or more) condensates so that W=0W=0 at the minimum. Then one would have (under the conditions mentioned above) a set of holomorphic equations for the ZZ-moduli which will always have a solution. However once supersymmetry is broken this option is no-longer available since now one needs to have W≠0W\neq 0 at the minimum if one is to have any hope of fine-tuning the cosmological constant to zero. However now the equations for the ZZ-moduli are a set of real non-linear equations which are not guaranteed to have a solution.

2.2 Corrections beyond leading order

As explained in the previous section, in smooth heterotic compactifications with hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 complex structure moduli not fixed by the holomorphicity of the gauge bundle, these ZZ-moduli cannot be frozen at tree-level by turning on a quantised background flux since this stabilisation would need |W0|≠0|W_{0}|\neq 0 which, in turn, would induce a dilaton and volume runaway. Thus, one has to look at any possible correction beyond the leading order expressions. Before presenting a brief summary of the various effects to be taken into account (perturbative and non-perturbative in both α′\alpha^{\prime} and gsg_{s}), let us mention two well-known control issues in heterotic constructions:

  • •

    Tension between weak coupling and large volume: In order to have full control over the effective field theory, one would like to stabilise the moduli in a region of field space where both perturbative and higher derivative corrections are small, i.e. respectively for gs≪1g_{s}\ll 1 and 𝒱≫1{\cal V}\gg 1. However, as we have already pointed out, this can be the case only if the 4D coupling is hyper-weak, in contrast with phenomenological observations. In fact, we have:

    gs2𝒱=αG​U​T≃125,\frac{g_{s}^{2}}{{\cal V}}=\alpha_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}\simeq\frac{1}{25}\,, (12)

    and so if we require gs≲1g_{s}\lesssim 1, the CY volume cannot be very large, 𝒱≲25{\cal V}\lesssim 25, implying that one has never a solid parametric control over the approximations used to fix the moduli.

  • •

    Tension between GUT scale and large volume: In heterotic constructions, the unification scale is identified with the Kaluza-Klein scale, MG​U​T=MK​KM_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}=M_{\scriptscriptstyle KK}, which cannot be lowered that much below the string scale for 𝒱≲25{\cal V}\lesssim 25, resulting in a GUT scale which is generically higher than the value inferred from the 1-loop running of the MSSM gauge couplings. In more detail, the string scale Ms≡ℓs−1M_{s}\equiv\ell_{s}^{-1} can be expressed in terms of the 4D Planck scale from dimensional reduction as (see appendix A for an explicit derivation):

    Ms2=MP24​π​αG​U​T−1≃MP2100​π≃(1.35⋅1017​GeV)2.M_{s}^{2}=\frac{M_{P}^{2}}{4\pi\alpha_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}^{-1}}\simeq\frac{M_{P}^{2}}{100\pi}\simeq\left(1.35\cdot 10^{17}\,\text{GeV}\right)^{2}\,. (13)

    In the case of an isotropic compactification, the Kaluza-Klein scale takes the form:

    MG​U​T=MK​K≃Ms𝒱1/6≳8⋅1016​GeVfor𝒱≲25,M_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}=M_{\scriptscriptstyle KK}\simeq\frac{M_{s}}{{\cal V}^{1/6}}\gtrsim 8\cdot 10^{16}\,{\rm GeV}\qquad\text{for}\qquad{\cal V}\lesssim 25\,, (14)

    which is clearly above the phenomenological value MG​U​T≃2.1⋅1016M_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}\simeq 2.1\cdot 10^{16} GeV. On the other hand, anisotropic compactifications with dd large dimensions of size L=x​ℓsL=x\ell_{s} with x≫1x\gg 1 and (6−d)(6-d) small dimensions of string size l=ℓsl=\ell_{s}, can lower the Kaluza-Klein scale:

    Vol⁡(X)=Ld​l6−d=xd​ℓs6=𝒱​ℓs6⇒MG​U​T=MK​K≃Msx≃Ms𝒱1/d.{\rm Vol}(X)=L^{d}l^{6-d}=x^{d}\ell_{s}^{6}={\cal V}\,\ell_{s}^{6}\quad\Rightarrow\quad M_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}=M_{\scriptscriptstyle KK}\simeq\frac{M_{s}}{x}\simeq\frac{M_{s}}{{\cal V}^{1/d}}\,. (15)

    For the case d=2d=2, one would get the encouraging result MG​U​T=Ms𝒱≳2.7⋅1016M_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}=\frac{M_{s}}{\sqrt{{\cal V}}}\gtrsim 2.7\cdot 10^{16} GeV.

2.2.1 Higher derivative effects

Let us start considering higher derivative effects, i.e. perturbative α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections to the Kähler potential. In the case of the standard embedding corresponding to (2,2)(2,2) worldsheet theories, the leading α′\alpha^{\prime} correction arises at 𝒪⁡(α′3)​ℛ4\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 3})\mathcal{R}^{4} [24] and depends on the CY Euler number χ⁡(X)=2​(h1,1−h1,2)\chi(X)=2\left(h^{1,1}-h^{1,2}\right). Its form can be derived by substituting the α′\alpha^{\prime} corrected volume 𝒱→𝒱+ξ/2{\cal V}\to{\cal V}+\xi/2 into the tree-level expression (3) with ξ=−ζ(3)χ(X)/(2(2π)3)\xi=-\zeta(3)\chi(X)/(2(2\pi)^{3}). Given that ζ⁡(3)≃1.2\zeta(3)\simeq 1.2, ξ\xi is of the order ξ≃(h1,2−h1,1)/200≃𝒪⁡(1)\xi\simeq\left(h^{1,2}-h^{1,1}\right)/200\simeq\mathcal{O}(1) for ordinary CY three-folds with (h1,2−h1,1)≃𝒪⁡(100)\left(h^{1,2}-h^{1,1}\right)\simeq\mathcal{O}(100). Hence for 𝒱≃𝒪⁡(20){\cal V}\simeq\mathcal{O}(20), the ratio ξ/(2​𝒱)≃𝒪⁡(1/40)\xi/(2{\cal V})\simeq\mathcal{O}(1/40) is a small number which justifies the expansion:

K≃−ln⁡𝒱−ξ2​𝒱⇒Kα′3=−ξ2​𝒱.K\simeq-\ln{\cal V}-\frac{\xi}{2{\cal V}}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad K_{\alpha^{\prime 3}}=-\frac{\xi}{2{\cal V}}\,. (16)

As pointed out in [23] however, this is the leading order higher derivative effect only for the standard embedding since (0,2)(0,2) worldsheet theories admit α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections already at 𝒪⁡(α′2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}) which deform the Kähler form JJ as:

J→J′=J+𝒪⁡(α′)​h~+𝒪⁡(α′2)​h~(2)+…,J\to J^{\prime}=J+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime})\,\tilde{h}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 2})\,\tilde{h}^{(2)}+...\,, (17)

where both h~\tilde{h} and h~(2)\tilde{h}^{(2)} are moduli-dependent (1,1)(1,1)-forms which are orthogonal to JJ, i.e. ∫X∗J∧h~=∫X∗J∧h~(2)=0\int_{X}\ast J\wedge\tilde{h}=\int_{X}\ast J\wedge\tilde{h}^{(2)}=0. Plugging J′J^{\prime} into the tree-level expression for KK (3) and then expanding, one finds that the 𝒪⁡(α′)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime}) correction vanishes because of the orthogonality between h~\tilde{h} and JJ whereas at 𝒪⁡(α′2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}) one finds:55 5 In looking at the derivation of the correction at 𝒪⁡(α′2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}) in [23], one may wonder about the rôle of field redefinitions. The fact that the corrected Kähler potential K′K^{\prime} can be written in terms of J′J^{\prime} as a function of ∫J′∧J′∧J′\int J^{\prime}\wedge J^{\prime}\wedge J^{\prime} alone, just the same way as the tree-level KK in terms of JJ, may imply that a field redefinition of the Kähler form may actually fully absorb the correction at 𝒪⁡(α′2){\cal O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}). To this end, the observation in [23] that the generically non-vanishing string 1-loop corrections in type IIB appearing at 𝒪⁡(α′2){\cal O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}) are S-dual to the heterotic correction, provides additional evidence for the existence of this term.

Kα′2=12​𝒱∫X∗h~∧h~=‖h~‖22​𝒱.K_{\alpha^{\prime 2}}=\frac{1}{2{\cal V}}\int_{X}\ast\tilde{h}\wedge\tilde{h}=\frac{||\tilde{h}||^{2}}{2{\cal V}}\,. (18)

Note that the correction (18) is generically leading with respect to (16) since (18) should be more correctly rewritten as:

Kα′2=g𝒱2/3withg≡‖h~‖22​𝒱1/3=−12​𝒱1/3∫XJ∧h~∧h~≥0,K_{\alpha^{\prime 2}}=\frac{g}{{\cal V}^{2/3}}\qquad\text{with}\qquad g\equiv\frac{||\tilde{h}||^{2}}{2{\cal V}^{1/3}}=-\frac{1}{2{\cal V}^{1/3}}\int_{X}J\wedge\tilde{h}\wedge\tilde{h}\geq 0\,, (19)

where gg is a homogeneous function of the Kähler moduli of degree 0 given that JJ scales as J∼𝒱1/3J\sim{\cal V}^{1/3} and h~\tilde{h} does not depend on 𝒱{\cal V}. As an illustrative example, let us consider the simplest Swiss-cheese CY XX with one large two-cycle tbt_{b} and one small blow-up mode tst_{s} so that J=tb​D^b−ts​D^sJ=t_{b}\hat{D}_{b}-t_{s}\hat{D}_{s} and the volume reads:

𝒱=kb​tb3−ks​ts3>0for0≤tstb<(kbks)1/3.{\cal V}=k_{b}t_{b}^{3}-k_{s}t_{s}^{3}>0\qquad\text{for}\qquad 0\leq\frac{t_{s}}{t_{b}}<\left(\frac{k_{b}}{k_{s}}\right)^{1/3}\,. (20)

In the limit kb​tb3≫ks​ts3k_{b}t_{b}^{3}\gg k_{s}t_{s}^{3}, the function gg then becomes (considering, without loss of generality, h~\tilde{h} as moduli-independent):

g=cb+cststb≥0withcb=−12​kb1/3∫XD^b∧h~∧h~andcs=12​kb1/3∫XD^s∧h~∧h~.g=c_{b}+c_{s}\,\frac{t_{s}}{t_{b}}\geq 0\qquad\text{with}\quad c_{b}=-\frac{1}{2\,k_{b}^{1/3}}\int_{X}\hat{D}_{b}\wedge\tilde{h}\wedge\tilde{h}\quad\text{and}\quad c_{s}=\frac{1}{2\,k_{b}^{1/3}}\int_{X}\hat{D}_{s}\wedge\tilde{h}\wedge\tilde{h}\,. (21)

The sign of cbc_{b} and csc_{s} can be constrained as follows. In the limit ts/tb→0t_{s}/t_{b}\to 0, gg reduces to g=cb=|cb|≥0g=c_{b}=|c_{b}|\geq 0. On the other hand, requiring that gg is semi-positive definite for any point in Kähler moduli space one finds:

cs=−|cb|​(kskb)1/3+|κ|,c_{s}=-\,|c_{b}|\,\left(\frac{k_{s}}{k_{b}}\right)^{1/3}+|\kappa|\,, (22)

where |κ||\kappa| is a semi-positive definite quantity.

2.2.2 Loop effects

Let us now focus on gsg_{s} perturbative effects which can modify both the Kähler potential and the gauge kinetic function. The exact expression of the string loop corrections to the Kähler potential is not known due to the difficulty in computing string scattering amplitudes on CY backgrounds. However, in the case of type IIB compactifications, these corrections have been argued to be sub-leading compared to α′\alpha^{\prime} effects by considering the results for simple toroidal orientifolds [47] and trying to generalise them to arbitrary CY backgrounds [48, 49]. Following [49], we shall try to estimate the behaviour of string loop corrections to the scalar potential by demanding that these match the Coleman-Weinberg potential:

Vgs≃Λ2​Str​M2≃m3/22​MK​K2≃|W|22​s​MP4𝒱2​(1+1/d),V_{g_{s}}\simeq\Lambda^{2}\,{\rm Str}\,M^{2}\simeq m_{3/2}^{2}\,M_{\scriptscriptstyle KK}^{2}\simeq\frac{|W|^{2}}{2s}\frac{M_{P}^{4}}{{\cal V}^{2(1+1/d)}}\,, (23)

where we took the cut-off scale Λ=MK​K\Lambda=M_{\scriptscriptstyle KK} and we considered dd arbitrary large dimensions. Note that these effects are indeed subdominant with respect to the α′\alpha^{\prime} ones for large volume since the 𝒪⁡(α′2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}) and 𝒪⁡(α′3)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 3}) corrections, (19) and (16), give respectively a contribution to the scalar potential of the order Vα′2≃|W|2/𝒱5/3V_{\alpha^{\prime 2}}\simeq|W|^{2}/{\cal V}^{5/3} and Vα′3≃|W|2/𝒱2V_{\alpha^{\prime 3}}\simeq|W|^{2}/{\cal V}^{2}, whereas the gsg_{s} potential (23) scales as Vgs≃|W|2/𝒱7/3V_{g_{s}}\simeq|W|^{2}/{\cal V}^{7/3} for the isotropic case with d=6d=6 and Vgs≃|W|2/𝒱3V_{g_{s}}\simeq|W|^{2}/{\cal V}^{3} for the anisotropic case with d=2d=2. Due to this subdominant behaviour of the string loop effects, we shall neglect them in what follows.

String loops correct also the gauge kinetic function (5). The 1-loop correction has a different expression for the visible and hidden E8E_{8} sectors [22]:

fvis=S+βi2​Ti,fhid=S−βi2​Ti,f_{\rm vis}=S+\frac{\beta_{i}}{2}\,T_{i}\,,\qquad f_{\rm hid}=S-\frac{\beta_{i}}{2}\,T_{i}\,, (24)

where:

βi=14​π​∫X(c2​(Vvis)−c2​(Vhid))∧D^i.\beta_{i}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{X}\left(c_{2}(V_{\rm vis})-c_{2}(V_{\rm hid})\right)\wedge\hat{D}_{i}\,. (25)

2.2.3 Non-perturbative effects

The 4D effective action receives also non-perturbative corrections in both α′\alpha^{\prime} and gsg_{s}. The α′\alpha^{\prime} effects are worldsheet instantons wrapping an internal two-cycle TiT_{i}. These give a contribution to the superpotential of the form:

Wwi=∑jBj​e−bi​j​Ti.W_{\rm wi}=\sum_{j}B_{j}\,e^{-\,b_{ij}T_{i}}\,. (26)

Note that these contributions arise only for (0,2)(0,2) worldsheet theories whereas they are absent in the case of the standard embedding. On the other hand, gsg_{s} non-perturbative effects include gaugino condensation and NS5 instantons. In the case of gaugino condensation in the hidden sector group, the resulting superpotential looks like:

Wgc=∑jAj​e−aj​fhid=∑jAj​e−aj​(S−βi2​Ti),W_{\rm gc}=\sum_{j}A_{j}\,e^{-\,a_{j}\,f_{\rm hid}}=\sum_{j}A_{j}\,e^{-\,a_{j}\left(S-\frac{\beta_{i}}{2}T_{i}\right)}\,, (27)

where in the absence of hidden sector U⁡(1)U(1) factors, all the hidden sector gauge groups have the same gauge kinetic function. Finally, NS5 instantons wrapping the whole CY manifold would give a sub-leading non-perturbative superpotential suppressed by e−𝒱≪1e^{-{\cal V}}\ll 1, and so we shall neglect them.

2.3 Moduli-dependent Fayet-Iliopoulos terms

As already pointed out, we shall allow line bundles in the visible sector where we turn on a vector bundle of the form Vvis=Uvis​⨁κℒκV_{{\rm vis}}=U_{\rm vis}\bigoplus_{\kappa}\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}. The presence of anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) factors induces U⁡(1)U(1) charges for the moduli in order to cancel the anomalies and gives rise to moduli-dependent Fayet-Iliopoulos (FI) terms. In particular, the charges of the Kähler moduli and the dilaton under the κ\kappa-th anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) read:

qTi(κ)=4​c1i​(ℒκ)andqs(κ)=2​γ(κ)=2​βi​c1i​(ℒκ),q^{(\kappa)}_{T_{i}}=4\,c_{1}^{i}(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa})\qquad\text{and}\qquad q_{s}^{(\kappa)}=2\,\gamma_{(\kappa)}=2\,\beta_{i}\,c_{1}^{i}(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa})\,, (28)

so that the FI-terms become [22]:

ξ(κ)=−qTi(κ)​∂K∂Ti−qs(κ)​∂K∂S=c1i​(ℒκ)𝒱​ki​j​k​tj​tk+γ(κ)s.\xi_{(\kappa)}=-q^{(\kappa)}_{T_{i}}\frac{\partial K}{\partial T_{i}}-q_{s}^{(\kappa)}\frac{\partial K}{\partial S}=\frac{c_{1}^{i}(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa})}{{\cal V}}\,k_{ijk}t_{j}t_{k}+\frac{\gamma_{(\kappa)}}{s}\,. (29)

Note that the dilaton-dependent term in the previous expression is a 1-loop correction to the FI-terms which at tree-level depend just on the Kähler moduli. The final D-term potential takes the form:

VD=∑κξ(κ)2Re⁡(f(κ)).V_{D}=\sum_{\kappa}\frac{\xi_{(\kappa)}^{2}}{{\rm Re}\left(f_{(\kappa)}\right)}\,. (30)

From the expressions (28) for the U⁡(1)U(1)-charges of the moduli, we can now check the U⁡(1)U(1)-invariance of the non-perturbative superpotentials (26) and (27). In the absence of charged matter fields, the only way to obtain a gauge invariant worldsheet instanton is to choose the gauge bundle such that all the TiT_{i} appearing in WwiW_{\rm wi} are not charged, i.e. c1i​(ℒκ)=0c_{1}^{i}(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa})=0 ∀κ\forall\kappa and ∀i\forall i. The superpotential generated by gaugino condensation is instead automatically U⁡(1)U(1)-invariant by construction since all the anomalous U⁡(1)U(1)s are in the visible sector whereas gaugino condensation takes place in the hidden sector. Thus, the hidden sector gauge kinetic function is not charged under any anomalous U⁡(1)U(1):

qfhid(κ)=qs(κ)−βi2​qTi(κ)=2​(γ(κ)−βi​c1i​(ℒκ))=0.q_{f_{\rm hid}}^{(\kappa)}=q_{s}^{(\kappa)}-\frac{\beta_{i}}{2}\,q_{T_{i}}^{(\kappa)}=2\left(\gamma_{(\kappa)}-\beta_{i}c_{1}^{i}(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa})\right)=0\,. (31)

Before concluding this section, we recall that in supergravity the D-terms are proportional to the F-terms for W≠0W\neq 0. In fact, the total U⁡(1)U(1)-charge of the superpotential WW is given by qW(κ)=qi(κ)​Wi/W=0q^{(\kappa)}_{W}=q^{(\kappa)}_{i}W_{i}/W=0, and so one can write:

ξ(κ)=−qi(κ)​Ki=−qi(κ)​Di​WW=−qi(κ)​e−K/2W​Ki​j¯​F¯j¯,\xi_{(\kappa)}=-\,q_{i}^{(\kappa)}K_{i}=-\,q_{i}^{(\kappa)}\frac{D_{i}W}{W}=-\,q_{i}^{(\kappa)}\frac{e^{-K/2}}{W}\,K_{i\bar{j}}\bar{F}^{\bar{j}}\,, (32)

where the F-terms are defined as Fi=eK/2​Ki​j¯​Dj¯​W¯F^{i}=e^{K/2}K^{i\bar{j}}D_{\bar{j}}\bar{W}. Therefore if all the F-terms are vanishing with W≠0W\neq 0, the FI-terms are also all automatically zero without giving rise to independent moduli-fixing relations.

3 Supersymmetric vacua

In this section, we shall perform a systematic discussion of heterotic supersymmetric vacua starting from an analysis of the tree-level scalar potential and then including corrections beyond the leading order expressions.

3.1 Tree-level scalar potential

In [20], Strominger analysed the 10D equations of motion and worked out the necessary and sufficient conditions to obtain 𝒩=1\mathcal{N}=1 supersymmetry in 4D assuming a 10D space-time of the form M×XM\times X where MM is a maximally symmetric 4D space-time and XX is a compact 6D manifold:

  1. 1.

    MM is Minkowski;

  2. 2.

    XX is a complex manifold, i.e. the Nijenhuis tensor has to vanish;

  3. 3.

    There exists one globally defined holomorphic (3,0)(3,0)-form Ω\Omega which is closed, i.e. d​Ω=0d\Omega=0, and whose norm is related to the complex structure (1,1)(1,1)-form JJ as (up to a constant):66 6 The adjoint operator d†d^{\dagger} can be defined from the inner product ⟨ω,σ⟩=∫Xω∧∗σ\langle\omega,\sigma\rangle=\int_{X}\omega\wedge\ast\sigma as ⟨ωp,d​ωp−1⟩=⟨d†​ωp,ωp−1⟩\langle\omega_{p},d\omega_{p-1}\rangle=\langle d^{\dagger}\omega_{p},\omega_{p-1}\rangle. For an even dimensional manifold, as we have here, d†=−∗d∗d^{\dagger}=-\ast d\ast.

    d†J=i(∂−∂¯)ln||Ω||d^{\dagger}J=i(\partial-\bar{\partial})\ln||\Omega|| (33)
  4. 4.

    The background gauge field FF has to satisfy the Hermitian Yang-Mills equations:

    F(0,2)=F(2,0)=0andgi​j¯​Fi​j¯=0F_{(0,2)}=F_{(2,0)}=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad g^{i\bar{j}}F_{i\bar{j}}=0 (34)
  5. 5.

    The dilaton ϕ\phi and the warp factor AA have to satisfy (again up to a constant):77 7 We are writing the total metric as d​s2=e2​A​(y)​(gμ​ν​(x)​d​xμ​d​xν+gi​j​(y)​d​yi​d​yj)ds^{2}=e^{2A(y)}\left(g_{\mu\nu}(x)dx^{\mu}dx^{\nu}+g_{ij}(y)dy^{i}dy^{j}\right).

    ϕ⁡(y)=A⁡(y)=18​ln⁡‖Ω‖​(y)\phi(y)=A(y)=\frac{1}{8}\ln||\Omega||(y) (35)
  6. 6.

    The background three-form flux is given by:

    H=−i2(∂−∂¯)J,H=-\frac{i}{2}(\partial-\bar{\partial})J\,, (36)

    together with the Bianchi identity:

    d​H=−α′4​[tr⁡(F∧F)−tr⁡(R∧R)].dH=-\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{4}\left[{\rm tr}(F\wedge F)-{\rm tr}(R\wedge R)\right]. (37)

Some of the conditions listed above can be reformulated also in terms of constraints on the five torsional classes 𝒲i\mathcal{W}_{i}, i=1,…,5i=1,...,5 (for a review see [1, 39]). The second condition corresponds to 𝒲1=𝒲2=0\mathcal{W}_{1}=\mathcal{W}_{2}=0 implying that the torsional class τ\tau belongs to the space τ∈𝒲3⊕𝒲4⊕𝒲5\tau\in\mathcal{W}_{3}\oplus\mathcal{W}_{4}\oplus\mathcal{W}_{5}. This is the case of ‘Hermitian manifolds’. Moreover, the third condition above gives 𝒲5=−2​𝒲4=d​ln⁡‖Ω‖\mathcal{W}_{5}=-2\mathcal{W}_{4}=d\ln||\Omega|| implying that both 𝒲4\mathcal{W}_{4} and 𝒲5\mathcal{W}_{5} are exact real 1-forms. We shall focus on the simplest solution to 2​𝒲4+𝒲5=02\mathcal{W}_{4}+\mathcal{W}_{5}=0 which is 𝒲4=𝒲5=0\mathcal{W}_{4}=\mathcal{W}_{5}=0 corresponding to the case of ‘special-Hermitian manifolds’ where the dilaton and the warp factor are constant [39]. More general solutions involve a non-constant dilaton profile in the extra dimensions and 𝒲i≠0\mathcal{W}_{i}\neq 0 for i=4,5i=4,5 but we shall not consider this option [39].

Let us comment on the implications of the last Strominger condition (36) which for constant dilaton can be rewritten as H=−12∗dJH=-\frac{1}{2}\ast dJ. Using the Hodge decomposition theorem, the three-form HH can be expanded uniquely as:

H=Hharm+Hexact+Hco−exact,H=H_{\rm harm}+H_{\rm exact}+H_{\rm co-exact}\,, (38)

where HharmH_{\rm harm} is a harmonic form, HexactH_{\rm exact} is an exact form and Hco−exactH_{\rm co-exact} is a co-exact form which are all orthogonal to each other. Given that ∗dJ=−d†∗J\ast dJ=-d^{\dagger}\ast J, (36) implies that HH is a co-exact form, and so Hharm=Hexact=0H_{\rm harm}=H_{\rm exact}=0. Moreover, since d​JdJ is a (2,1)+(1,2)(2,1)+(1,2) form, (36) implies that the (3,0)+(0,3)(3,0)+(0,3) component of Hco−exactH_{\rm co-exact} is zero while the (2,1)+(1,2)(2,1)+(1,2) component breaks the Kähler condition d​J=0dJ=0. However this happens only at 𝒪⁡(α′)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime}). In fact, the general expression of the HH-flux is:

H=Hflux+d​B2−α′4​[CS⁡(A)−CS⁡(ω)],H=H_{\rm flux}+dB_{2}-\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{4}\left[{\rm CS}(A)-{\rm CS}(\omega)\right], (39)

where HfluxH_{\rm flux} is a harmonic piece and the combination of Chern-Simons three-forms can also be decomposed as:

[CS⁡(A)−CS⁡(ω)]=CSharm+CSexact+CSco−exact.\left[{\rm CS}(A)-{\rm CS}(\omega)\right]={\rm CS}_{\rm harm}+{\rm CS}_{\rm exact}+{\rm CS}_{\rm co-exact}\,. (40)

Comparing the two expressions for HH, (38) and (39), we have (due to the uniqueness of the Hodge decomposition):

Hharm=Hflux−α′4​CSharm,Hexact=d​B2−α′4​CSexact,Hco−exact=−α′4​CSco−exact.H_{\rm harm}=H_{\rm flux}-\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{4}\,{\rm CS}_{\rm harm}\,,\quad H_{\rm exact}=dB_{2}-\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{4}\,{\rm CS}_{\rm exact}\,,\quad H_{\rm co-exact}=-\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{4}\,{\rm CS}_{\rm co-exact}\,.

Then the relation (36) takes the form:

α′2CSco−exact=∗dJ,\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{2}\,{\rm CS}_{\rm co-exact}=\ast\,dJ\,, (41)

showing exactly that the Kähler condition d​J=0dJ=0 is violated at O⁡(α′)O(\alpha^{\prime}). Note that this would be the case for the non-standard embedding where CSco−exact≠0{\rm CS}_{\rm co-exact}\neq 0 contrary to the less generic situation of the standard embedding where the Chern-Simons piece vanishes. Taking the exterior derivative of (41) we recover the Bianchi identity (37) which now looks like:

d∗d​J=α′2​[tr⁡(F∧F)−tr⁡(R∧R)].d\ast dJ=\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{2}\,\left[{\rm tr}(F\wedge F)-{\rm tr}(R\wedge R)\right]. (42)

This 10D analysis can also be recast in terms of an effective potential which can be written as a sum of BPS-like terms and whose minimisation reproduces the conditions above [36, 41, 42, 43]. Furthermore, some of these conditions can be re-derived as F- or D-term equations of 4D supergravity, which could lead to the stabilisation of some of the moduli in a Minkowski vacuum. For example, it has been shown in [36, 43], that the second equation in (34) is equivalent to a D-term condition since:

∗61⋅gi​j¯Fi​j¯=12F∧J∧J.{\ast_{6}1\cdot}\,g^{i\bar{j}}F_{i\bar{j}}=\frac{1}{2}\,F\wedge J\wedge J\,. (43)

This D-term condition holds for general non-Abelian gauge fields. If we restrict to Abelian fluxes and integrate the above condition over the CY, this reproduces the tree-level expression for the Fayet-Iliopoulos terms given in (29). If we expand the Abelian fluxes as F(κ)=c1i​(ℒκ)​D^iF_{(\kappa)}=c_{1}^{i}(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa})\hat{D}_{i} together with J=tj​D^jJ=t^{j}\hat{D}_{j} we obtain:

ξ(κ)=1𝒱​∫XF(κ)∧J∧J=c1i​(ℒκ)𝒱​ki​j​k​tj​tk,\xi_{(\kappa)}=\frac{1}{{\cal V}}\int_{X}F_{(\kappa)}\wedge J\wedge J=\frac{c_{1}^{i}(\mathcal{L}_{\kappa})}{{\cal V}}\,k_{ijk}t_{j}t_{k}\,, (44)

which reproduces exactly the tree-level part of (29).

Regarding the F-terms, as we have seen in section 2.1, the starting point is the expression of the flux superpotential which has been inferred in [44] by comparing the dimensional reduction of the 10D coupling of HH to the gravitino mass term in the 4D supergravity action. The final result is:88 8 In [41] and [43] it is suggested that the complete expression for WW should more appropriately be W=∫X(H+i2​𝑑J)∧ΩW=\int_{X}(H+\frac{i}{2}\,dJ)\wedge\Omega, similarly to the type IIB case where one has the RR flux in addition to the HH-flux. Integrating by parts, the new piece can be rewritten as ∫XJ∧𝑑Ω\int_{X}J\wedge d\Omega which clearly vanishes since d​Ω=0d\Omega=0. However, if one considers the case where d​Ω≠0d\Omega\neq 0, i.e. where supersymmetry is broken directly at the 10D level, this integral would still be zero if the internal manifold is complex since d​JdJ is of Hodge type (2,1)+(1,2)(2,1)+(1,2) while Ω\Omega is (3,0)(3,0). Thus this term can play a useful rôle only for non-complex manifolds with broken supersymmetry. Due to the difficulty to study this case in a controlled way, we shall not consider it and neglect this additional piece.

Wflux=∫XH∧Ω=∫XHharm∧Ω.W_{\rm flux}=\int_{X}H\wedge\Omega=\int_{X}H_{\rm harm}\wedge\Omega\,. (45)

and similarly mq=∫AqHharmm_{q}=\int_{A_{q}}H_{\rm harm}. The quantities epe^{p} and mqm_{q} are integer flux quanta.

and expanding a generic element of the basis of harmonic (2,1)(2,1)-forms as χα​(Z,Z¯)=fαp​(Z,Z¯)​αp−gq,α​(Z,Z¯)​βq\chi_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})=f^{p}_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})\alpha_{p}-g_{q,\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})\beta^{q}, we find:

where we used again the orthogonality of the different Hodge components of HH and the fact that ∗χα=i​χα\ast\chi_{\alpha}={\rm i}\chi_{\alpha}. On the other hand, the dilaton and Kähler moduli F-terms look like:

Due to the no-scale cancellation, these F-terms give rise to a scalar potential which is positive definite and reads:

Let us now set all the F-terms to zero and see what they correspond to:

  • •

    DZα​Wflux=0D_{Z^{\alpha}}W_{\rm flux}=0 implies that the (2,1)+(1,2)(2,1)+(1,2) component of HharmH_{\rm harm} is zero.

  • •

    DS​Wflux=0D_{S}W_{\rm flux}=0 and DTi​Wflux=0D_{T_{i}}W_{\rm flux}=0 imply that the (3,0)+(0,3)(3,0)+(0,3) component of HharmH_{\rm harm} should also be zero, i.e. W0≡⟨Wflux⟩=0W_{0}\equiv\langle W_{\rm flux}\rangle=0, if one wants to avoid solutions with a dilaton run-away (s→∞s\to\infty) or where the internal space decompactifies (𝒱→∞{\cal V}\to\infty).

Combining these two solutions, one has that the total harmonic piece of HH should vanish and is of course consistent with the Strominger condition (36). An important question to ask now is whether these conditions allow for the fixing of some moduli. The answer is no. Let us see why.

The first condition DZα​W=0D_{Z^{\alpha}}W=0 appears to fix the complex structure moduli supersymmetrically since one obtains as many equations, bα​(Z,Z¯)=0b_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})=0, as the number of unknowns (assuming that the 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} real equations have solutions for some sets of values of the 2​h1,2+22\,h^{1,2}+2 fluxes). The second condition W0≡⟨Wflux⟩=i​a​(Z)=0W_{0}\equiv\langle W_{\rm flux}\rangle={\rm i}\,{a}({Z})=0 could then be satisfied by an appropriate choice of flux quanta.

However the two conditions DZα​W=0D_{Z^{\alpha}}W=0 ⇔\Leftrightarrow bα​(Z,Z¯)=0b_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})=0 ∀α\forall\alpha and W0=0W_{0}=0 ⇔\Leftrightarrow a⁡(Z)=0a(Z)=0 imply from (46) that Hharm=0H_{\rm harm}=0. Given that HH does not depend on the complex structure moduli, this implies that all flux quanta are zero. In turn, (49) and (50) are both identically zero, and so no potential for the ZZ-moduli is developed. Therefore no moduli, not even the complex structure ones, can be stabilised at tree-level by using quantised background fluxes.99 9 The corresponding situation in type IIB is very different since there are two types of fluxes and the effective flux G3G_{3} is complex [40]. In particular, this implies that one cannot perform a two-step stabilisation (similarly to type IIB) where at tree-level the ZZ-moduli are fixed supersymmetrically while the SS- and TT-moduli are kept flat by tuning W0=0W_{0}=0, and then these remaining moduli are lifted by quantum corrections. As we have already pointed out in section 2.1, we shall avoid this problem by considering in the next section situations with non-zero flux quanta which allow to fix the ZZ-moduli with W0≠0W_{0}\neq 0. The dilaton and volume runaway is then prevented by scanning over integral and fractional fluxes which give a value of W0W_{0} small enough to compete with non-perturbative effects. Hence the system becomes stable only when non-perturbative effects are included, implying that all the moduli get stabilised beyond tree-level.

3.1.1 Chern-Simons action and gauge bundle moduli

In this section, we shall show that also the first equation in (34), i.e. F(0,2)=F(2,0)=0F_{(0,2)}=F_{(2,0)}=0, can be derived from an F-term condition in 4D supergravity. This requires a brief discussion of gauge bundle moduli. Let us focus on the Chern-Simons piece of the flux superpotential:

WCS​[A]=∫XTr⁡(A∧𝑑A+23​A∧A∧A)∧Ω.W_{\rm CS}[A]=\int_{X}{\rm Tr}\left(A\wedge dA+\frac{2}{3}\,A\wedge A\wedge A\right)\wedge\Omega\,. (53)

In the previous expression AA is a function of both xx and yy, i.e. non-compact and compact coordinates respectively, but the differentiation is just d=dym∂md=dy^{m}\partial_{m} since we are only interested in the contribution to the 4D scalar potential. We shall now write the gauge potential as:

A⁡(x,y)=A0​(y)+Adef​(x,y),A(x,y)=A_{0}(y)+A_{\rm def}(x,y)\,, (54)

where A0A_{0} is a background contribution independent of xx and AdefA_{\rm def} is a generic deformation which can be parameterised as:

Adef​(x,y)=∑I=1∞CI​(x)​ωI​(y),A_{\rm def}(x,y)=\sum_{I=1}^{\infty}C_{I}(x)\omega^{I}(y)\,, (55)

where CIC_{I} are 4D scalar fields and ωI\omega^{I} are an infinite set of 11-forms living on XX and valued in the adjoint representation of the structure group of the gauge bundle defined by A0A_{0}.1010 10 We expect the set of 11-forms ωI\omega^{I} to be discrete since they will be solutions to an elliptic differential equation on the compact manifold.

The superpotential (53) then becomes the sum of a constant, a linear, a quadratic and a cubic term in the CC’s:

WCS=WCS,(0)+WCS,(1)I​CI+WCS,(2)I​J​CI​CJ+WCS,(3)I​J​K​CI​CJ​CK,W_{\rm CS}=W_{{\rm CS},(0)}+W_{{\rm CS},(1)}^{I}C_{I}+W_{{\rm CS},(2)}^{IJ}C_{I}C_{J}+W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{IJK}C_{I}C_{J}C_{K}\,, (56)

with (for notational simplicity we dropped the trace symbol):

WCS,(0)\displaystyle W_{{\rm CS},(0)} =\displaystyle= WCS​[A0],WCS,(1)I=2​∫XωI∧F0∧Ω,\displaystyle W_{\rm CS}[A_{0}]\,,\qquad W_{{\rm CS},(1)}^{I}=2\,\int_{X}\omega^{I}\wedge F_{0}\wedge\Omega\,, (57)
WCS,(2)I​J\displaystyle W_{{\rm CS},(2)}^{IJ} =\displaystyle= ∫XωI∧D¯0​ωJ∧Ω,WCS,(3)I​J​K=23​∫XωI∧ωJ∧ωK∧Ω,\displaystyle\int_{X}\omega^{I}\wedge\overline{D}_{0}\omega^{J}\wedge\Omega\,,\qquad W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{IJK}=\frac{2}{3}\int_{X}\omega^{I}\wedge\omega^{J}\wedge\omega^{K}\wedge\Omega\,, (58)

where the gauge covariant derivative D¯0\overline{D}_{0} is defined as D¯0​ω(0,p)=∂¯​ω(0,p)+A0∧ω(0,p)−(−1)p​ω(0,p)∧A0\overline{D}_{0}\omega_{(0,p)}=\overline{\partial}\omega_{(0,p)}+A_{0}\wedge\omega_{(0,p)}-(-1)^{p}\omega_{(0,p)}\wedge A_{0} for an arbitrary (0,p)(0,p)-form ω(0,p)\omega_{(0,p)}. Note that in order to derive these expressions we used d​Ω=0d\Omega=0, the anti-commutativity of dd and 11-forms and the cyclicity of the trace. As we have argued earlier, classically the total superpotential WW should be zero at the minimum (for all the moduli), and so the F-term equation for the bundle moduli CIC_{I} is:

0=FCI=∂WCS∂CI=WCS,(1)I+2​WCS,(2)I​J​CJ+2​WCS,(3)I​J​K​CJ​CK.0=F_{C_{I}}=\frac{\partial W_{\rm CS}}{\partial C_{I}}=W_{{\rm CS},(1)}^{I}+2W_{{\rm CS},(2)}^{IJ}C_{J}+2W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{IJK}C_{J}C_{K}\,. (59)

If AdefA_{\rm def} is a small deformation of the background A0A_{0}, i.e. CI​(x)=εI​(x)C_{I}(x)=\varepsilon_{I}(x), then these F-term equations can be solved order by order in ε\varepsilon, obtaining:

  • •

    At zeroth order FCI=0F_{C_{I}}=0 gives WCS,(1)I=0W_{{\rm CS},(1)}^{I}=0 ∀I\forall I which from (57) implies that the (0,2)(0,2)-component of the unperturbed field strength F0F_{0} has to vanish. Hence we recover the holomorphic Yang-Mills equation F0,(0,2)=0F_{0,(0,2)}=0 which determines (given a complex structure) A0A_{0} to be a flat (0,1)(0,1) connection. This bundle, which we call Q0Q_{0}, then determines the exterior derivative operator D¯0\overline{D}_{0}.

    This equation has two possible solutions:

    1. 1.

    The first solution defines the gauge bundle moduli which parameterise all possible deformations of the background that keep the gauge bundle holomorphic. These first order deformations correspond to ωi∈H1​(E​n​d​(Q0))\omega^{i}\in H^{1}(End(Q_{0})) where N≡dim⁡(H1​(E​n​d​(Q0)))N\equiv{\rm dim}\left(H^{1}(End(Q_{0}))\right) which is expected to be finite though it may change as one varies the complex structure since the equations determining the (0,1)(0,1)-forms ωi\omega^{i} depend on the ZZ-moduli. Hence NN is a function of the ZZ-moduli, i.e. N=N⁡(Z)N=N(Z). If N=0N=0 for Z=Z0Z=Z_{0}, then if the complex structure moduli can be stabilised via the fluxes exactly at Z=Z0Z=Z_{0}, the absence of any gauge bundle moduli is guaranteed (see [37] for similar considerations). We denoted as hhol1,2h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} the number of ZZ-moduli unconstrained by the equation D¯0​ωi​(Z)=0\overline{D}_{0}\omega^{i}(Z)=0, which represents the dimensionality of the sub-locus in complex structure moduli space where the gauge bundle is holomorphic. In the best case scenario where hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0 one does not need to turn on any harmonic flux to fix the ZZ-moduli, whereas in the more general case where hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 the remaining complex structure moduli can be fixed only by turning on a quantised background flux. For a graphical sketch of the ‘cross-structure’ of the combined complex structure and gauge bundle moduli space see Fig 1.

    The second solution of (60) implies that the forms ωι\omega^{\iota} are not closed under D¯0\overline{D}_{0} and the index ι\iota ranges over an infinite set of values. Hence CιC_{\iota} are not flat directions but correspond to massive deformations, namely the Kaluza-Klein modes. We can then easily realise that WCS,(2)ι​σW_{{\rm CS},(2)}^{\iota\sigma} gives the mass matrix for these Kaluza-Klein modes.

    showing that a possible obstruction to the presence of gauge bundle moduli can arise if the Yukawa couplings are different from zero, i.e. WCS,(3)i​j​k≠0W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{ijk}\neq 0 ∀i\forall i. We stress again the fact that WCS,(3)i​j​kW_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{ijk} is a function of the ZZ-moduli, and so even if the equation D¯0​ωi​(Z)=0\overline{D}_{0}\omega^{i}(Z)=0 (or the flux stabilisation) gives a solution Z=Z∗Z=Z_{\ast} such that N⁡(Z∗)≠0N(Z_{\ast})\neq 0, one could still fix all the CC-moduli if WCS,(3)i​j​k​(Z∗)≠0W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{ijk}(Z_{\ast})\neq 0 ∀i\forall i.

Having motivated both the background gauge flux and the nature of the leading deformation we can now work with an arbitrary deformation by separating the set {CI}={Ci(0)}⊕{CιKK}\{C_{I}\}=\{C^{(0)}_{i}\}\oplus\{C^{\rm KK}_{\iota}\} with the first set being the massless modes and the second the Kaluza-Klein modes. This corresponds to splitting the set of 1-forms as {ωI}={ω(0)i}⊕{ωKKι}\{\omega^{I}\}=\{\omega^{i}_{(0)}\}\oplus\{\omega^{\iota}_{\rm KK}\} where D¯0​ω(0)i=0\overline{D}_{0}\omega^{i}_{(0)}=0 while D¯0​ωKKι≠0\overline{D}_{0}\omega^{\iota}_{\rm KK}\neq 0. Then under the condition F0,(0,2)=0F_{0,(0,2)}=0, the F-term equations (59) take the form:

0=FCi(0)=2​WCS,(3)i​k​l​Ck(0)​Cl(0)+4​WCS,(3)i​k​λ​Ck(0)​CλKK+2​WCS,(3)i​σ​λ​CσKK​CλKK,0=F_{C_{i}^{(0)}}=2W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{ikl}C_{k}^{(0)}C_{l}^{(0)}+4W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{ik\lambda}C_{k}^{(0)}C_{\lambda}^{\rm KK}+2W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{i\sigma\lambda}C_{\sigma}^{\rm KK}C_{\lambda}^{\rm KK}\,, (62)

and:

0=FCιKK=2​WCS,(2)ι​σ​CσKK+2​WCS,(3)ι​k​l​Ck(0)​Cl(0)+4​WCS,(3)ι​k​λ​Ck(0)​CλKK+2​WCS,(3)ι​σ​λ​CσKK​CλKK.0=F_{C_{\iota}^{\rm KK}}=2W_{{\rm CS},(2)}^{\iota\sigma}C_{\sigma}^{\rm KK}+2W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{\iota kl}C_{k}^{(0)}C_{l}^{(0)}+4W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{\iota k\lambda}C_{k}^{(0)}C_{\lambda}^{\rm KK}+2W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{\iota\sigma\lambda}C_{\sigma}^{\rm KK}C_{\lambda}^{\rm KK}\,. (63)

Note that WCS,(2)ι​σ≡MKKι​σW_{{\rm CS},(2)}^{\iota\sigma}\equiv M^{\iota\sigma}_{\rm KK} is the mass matrix for the Kaluza-Klein modes which by definition is non-singular. So eq. (63) can be solved for the massive modes in terms of the massless modes giving a relation of the form:

CσKK=[MKK]σ​λ−1​WCS,(3)λ​m​n​Cm(0)​Cn(0)+O⁡(C03).C^{\rm KK}_{\sigma}=[M_{\rm KK}]^{-1}_{\sigma\lambda}W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{\lambda mn}C^{(0)}_{m}C^{(0)}_{n}+O(C_{0}^{3})\,. (64)

Using this in (62) we get the massless field equation which is the generalisation of (61) for arbitrarily large deformations of the background gauge bundle:

2​WCS,(3)i​k​l​Ck(0)​Cl(0)+O⁡(C(0)3)=0.2W_{{\rm CS},(3)}^{ikl}C^{(0)}_{k}C^{(0)}_{l}+O(C_{(0)}^{3})=0\,. (65)

These field equations always admit the solution Ck(0)=0C_{k}^{(0)}=0 for all gauge bundle moduli which leaves the complex structure moduli unfixed in the absence of harmonic quantised flux. Moreover, this solution remains valid even in the presence of non-zero WW since the additional term in DC​WD_{C}W is proportional to CC. However one could also have solutions with non-zero VEVs for the CC-moduli which could be obtained by cancelling field-dependent FI-terms associated with anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) factors. By the cross structure of the combined moduli space [33, 34, 35], this in turn implies stabilisation of at most h1,2−hhol1,2h^{1,2}-h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} complex structure moduli. This situation is particularly relevant for the case of heterotic orbifold compactifications which often have only a few untwisted ZZ-moduli. In this case it seems possible to stabilise all gauge bundle moduli and the small total number of untwisted complex structure moduli using only higher-order terms in (65) and a sufficient number of D-terms from anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) factors [4, 5, 6, 7, 8].

In the rest of the paper we will focus on the generic situation where this stabilisation procedure fixes all the gauge bundle moduli and some, but not all, complex structure moduli, so that hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 ZZ-moduli are still left flat. Furthermore, even if hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0, it could still be that some CC-moduli are fixed at zero VEV, implying that the complex structure moduli could still be flat (see Fig. 1).

3.2 Corrections beyond tree-level

Given that the remaining hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 ZZ-moduli cannot be fixed at tree-level by using quantised fluxes (since |W0|≠0|W_{0}|\neq 0 would induce a runaway for both ss and 𝒱{\cal V}), let us focus on perturbative and non-perturbative corrections to the scalar potential. We shall proceed in two steps, showing first how to fix the complex structure moduli and the dilaton by the inclusion of an SS-dependent gaugino condensate, and then explaining how to stabilise the Kähler moduli by an interplay of world-sheet instantons and threshold corrections to the gauge kinetic function. For the time being, we shall neglect perturbative corrections to the Kähler potential (either α′\alpha^{\prime} or gsg_{s}) since these generically break supersymmetry, and so we shall include them only in section 4 where we shall study supersymmetry breaking vacua.

3.2.1 Step 1: ZZ and SS stabilisation by gaugino condensation

Let us add a single SS-dependent gaugino condensate to the superpotential and determine how this term modifies the tree-level picture:

W=Wflux+Wgc=∫XH∧Ω+A⁡(Z)​e−λ​S.W=W_{\rm flux}+W_{\rm gc}=\int_{X}H\wedge\Omega+A(Z)\,e^{-\lambda S}\,. (66)

The Kähler-covariant derivatives now become:

DZα​W\displaystyle D_{Z^{\alpha}}W =\displaystyle= i​bα​(Z)+e−λ​S​[∂αA⁡(Z)−kα​(Z,Z¯)​A​(Z)],\displaystyle{\rm i}\,b_{\alpha}(Z)+e^{-\lambda S}\left[\partial_{\alpha}A(Z)-k_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})A(Z)\right], (67)
DS​W\displaystyle D_{S}W =\displaystyle= −12​s​[i​a​(Z)+(2​λ​s+1)​A​(Z)​e−λ​S],\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2s}\left[{\rm i}\,a(Z)+(2\lambda s+1)A(Z)\,e^{-\lambda S}\right], (68)
DTi​W\displaystyle D_{T_{i}}W =\displaystyle= −i​a​(Z)+A⁡(Z)​e−λ​S4​𝒱​ki​j​k​tj​tk.\displaystyle-\frac{{\rm i}\,a(Z)+A(Z)\,e^{-\lambda S}}{4{\cal V}}\,k_{ijk}t_{j}t_{k}\,. (69)

The potential is again of the no-scale type (i.e. given by the first equality of (52)). At the minimum the complex structure moduli will be frozen at the solution to:

DZαW=0⇔ibα(Z)=e−λ​S[kα(Z,Z¯)A(Z)−∂αA(Z)],D_{Z^{\alpha}}W=0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad{\rm i}\,b_{\alpha}(Z)=e^{-\lambda S}\left[k_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})A(Z)-\partial_{\alpha}A(Z)\right], (70)

and now the dilaton is not forced anymore to run-away to infinity:

DSW=0⇔W0≡ia(Z)=−(2λs+1)A(Z)e−λ​S.D_{S}W=0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad W_{0}\equiv{\rm i}\,a(Z)=-(2\lambda s+1)A(Z)\,e^{-\lambda S}\,. (71)

The potential for the Kähler moduli is flat, resulting in a Minkowski vacuum with broken supersymmetry since substituting (71) into (69) one finds:

DTi​W=−(2​λ​s2​λ​s+1)​W04​𝒱​ki​j​k​tj​tk.D_{T_{i}}W=-\left(\frac{2\lambda s}{2\lambda s+1}\right)\frac{W_{0}}{4{\cal V}}\,k_{ijk}t_{j}t_{k}\,. (72)

The previous expression for W0≠0W_{0}\neq 0, finite volume and ti>1t_{i}>1 ∀i\forall i, gives DTi​W≠0D_{T_{i}}W\neq 0 for a generic point in moduli space.

Let us comment now on the possibility to satisfy (71) at the physical point ⟨s⟩≃2\langle s\rangle\simeq 2 that corresponds to αG​U​T−1≃25\alpha_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}^{-1}\simeq 25. Setting A=1A=1 and λ=8​π2/N\lambda=8\pi^{2}/N where NN is the rank of the S​U​(N)SU(N) condensing gauge group, we have (fixing the axion aa at λ​⟨a⟩=π\lambda\langle a\rangle=\pi):

W0=(16​π2​⟨s⟩N+1)​e−8​π2N​⟨s⟩.W_{0}=\left(\frac{16\pi^{2}\langle s\rangle}{N}+1\right)\,e^{-\frac{8\pi^{2}}{N}\langle s\rangle}\,. (73)

As an illustrative example, for ⟨s⟩≃2\langle s\rangle\simeq 2 and N=5N=5, the previous expression would give W0≃10−12W_{0}\simeq 10^{-12}, which for 𝒱≃20{\cal V}\simeq 20 corresponds to a gravitino mass of the order m3/2=W0/(2​s​𝒱)≃330m_{3/2}=W_{0}/(\sqrt{2s{\cal V}})\simeq 330 TeV. On the other hand, for N=30N=30 (as in the case of E8E_{8}), one would obtain W0≃0.06W_{0}\simeq 0.06 corresponding to a GUT-scale gravitino mass: m3/2≃1016m_{3/2}\simeq 10^{16} GeV. Due to the absence of Ramond-Ramond fluxes, there is in general no freedom to tune the heterotic flux superpotential W0W_{0} to values much smaller than unity, implying that heterotic CY compactifications generically predict a gravitino mass close to the GUT scale. As we already pointed out, low-energy supersymmetry could instead be obtained in the particular cases when hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0 so that one does not need to turn on W0≠0W_{0}\neq 0 to fix all the ZZ-moduli, in orbifold constructions or in compactifications on non-complex manifolds.

A possible way to obtain fractional values of W0W_{0} of order 0.1−0.010.1-0.01 has been described in [17] where the authors considered a trivial B2B_{2} field and a rigid 3-cycle Σ3\Sigma_{3} such that the integral of HH over Σ3\Sigma_{3} (ignoring the contribution from the spin connection):

∫Σ3H≃−∫Σ3CS(A),\int_{\Sigma_{3}}H\simeq-\int_{\Sigma_{3}}{\rm CS}(A)\,, (74)

gives rise to a fractional flux.1111 11 Note that these flux quanta are well-defined quantities even if HH is not closed since a rigid homology class admits just one representative Stabilisation of all complex structure moduli would then require scanning the three-form flux over all cycles to search for VEVs ⟨Zα⟩\langle Z_{\alpha}\rangle such that the overall (0,3)(0,3)-contribution to the superpotential (45) is of the order of the fractional Chern-Simons contribution or smaller.1212 12 For the purpose of an explicit demonstration of such vacua one may rely on CYs arising in Greene-Plesser pairs of manifolds related by mirror symmetry [51, 52, 53]. CY mirror pairs arising from the Greene-Plesser construction have their complex structure moduli space partitioned by a typically large discrete symmetry Γ\Gamma into an invariant subspace and its complement. One can then show that the periods of the invariant subspace depend at higher-order non-trivially on all the Γ\Gamma-non-invariant complex structure moduli. If the Γ\Gamma-invariant subspace is of low dimensionality (as is the case e.g. of the CY ℂ​ℙ111694​[18]\mathbb{CP}^{4}_{11169}[18] as discussed in [54, 55]), then turning on the relatively few fluxes on the invariant subspace is enough to stabilise all complex structure moduli at an isolated minimum [54, 55]. On such a CY manifold one can therefore stabilise all ZZ-moduli by just turning a few fractional Chern-Simons (0,3)(0,3)-type fluxes on the cycles of the invariant subspace, which can serve to demonstrate the existence of such vacua.

3.2.2 Step 2: TT stabilisation by worldsheet instantons and threshold effects

The Kähler moduli can develop a potential either by loop corrections to the gauge kinetic function or via worldsheet instantons. Let us start considering the case with just threshold effects.

Threshold effects: The potential generated by gaugino condensation takes the form:

Wgc=A⁡(Z)​e−λ⁡(S−βi2​Ti),W_{\rm gc}=A(Z)\,e^{-\lambda\left(S-\frac{\beta_{i}}{2}\,T_{i}\right)}\,, (75)

lifting the TT-moduli and modifying (72) into:

DTiW=−λ​W02​(2​λ​s+1)[βi+s𝒱ki​j​ktjtk]=0⇔βi=−s𝒱ki​j​ktjtk.D_{T_{i}}W=-\frac{\lambda\,W_{0}}{2(2\lambda s+1)}\left[\beta_{i}+\frac{s}{{\cal V}}\,k_{ijk}t_{j}t_{k}\right]=0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\beta_{i}=-\frac{s}{{\cal V}}\,k_{ijk}t_{j}t_{k}\,. (76)

This result, in turn, gives:

Re⁡(fhid1−loop)=−βi2​ti=s2​𝒱​ki​j​k​ti​tj​tk=3​s=3​Re​(fhidtree),{\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm hid}^{\rm 1-loop}\right)=-\frac{\beta_{i}}{2}\,t_{i}=\frac{s}{2{\cal V}}\,k_{ijk}t_{i}t_{j}t_{k}=3\,s=3\,{\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm hid}^{\rm tree}\right), (77)

implying that perturbation theory in the hidden sector is not under control since the one-loop contribution is bigger than the tree-level one. Moreover the gauge kinetic function of the visible sector becomes negative:

Re⁡(fvis)=gvis−2=s+βi2​ti=−2​s<0,{\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm vis}\right)=g_{\rm vis}^{-2}=s+\frac{\beta_{i}}{2}\,t_{i}=-2s<0\,, (78)

meaning that the positive tree-level contribution is driven to negative values by threshold effects. Actually, before becoming negative, gvis−2g_{\rm vis}^{-2} will vanish corresponding to a strong coupling transition whose understanding is not very clear [17]. Note that we neglected D-terms since, due to the relation (32), if present, they would also cause the same problems. Let us see now how these control issues can be addressed by including worldsheet instantons [19].

Threshold effects and worldsheet instantons: The new total non-perturbative superpotential reads:

Wnp=A⁡(Z)​e−λ⁡(S−βi2​Ti)+B⁡(Z)​e−μ​T∗,W_{\rm np}=A(Z)\,e^{-\lambda\left(S-\frac{\beta_{i}}{2}\,T_{i}\right)}+B(Z)\,e^{-\mu\,T_{\ast}}\,, (79)

where we included the contribution of a single worldsheet instanton dependent on T∗T_{\ast}. In general, one could have more non-perturbative α′\alpha^{\prime} contributions, but we shall here show that just one worldsheet instanton is enough to overcome the previous problems. The new Kähler covariant derivatives become:

DZα​W\displaystyle D_{Z^{\alpha}}W =\displaystyle= i​bα​(Z)+Wgc​[∂αA⁡(Z)A⁡(Z)−kα​(Z,Z¯)]+Wwi​[∂αB⁡(Z)B⁡(Z)−kα​(Z,Z¯)],\displaystyle{\rm i}\,b_{\alpha}(Z)+W_{\rm gc}\left[\frac{\partial_{\alpha}A(Z)}{A(Z)}-k_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})\right]+W_{\rm wi}\left[\frac{\partial_{\alpha}B(Z)}{B(Z)}-k_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})\right], (80)
DS​W\displaystyle D_{S}W =\displaystyle= −12​s​[W0+(2​λ​s+1)​Wgc+Wwi],\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2s}\left[W_{0}+(2\lambda s+1)W_{\rm gc}+W_{\rm wi}\right], (81)
DTp​W\displaystyle D_{T_{p}}W =\displaystyle= λβp2Wgc−W0+Wgc+Wwi4​𝒱kp​j​ktjtkp≠∗,\displaystyle\lambda\frac{\beta_{p}}{2}\,W_{\rm gc}-\frac{W_{0}+W_{\rm gc}+W_{\rm wi}}{4{\cal V}}\,k_{pjk}t_{j}t_{k}\qquad p\neq\ast\,, (82)

The solutions describing supersymmetric vacua with vanishing F-terms are:
