(91)

3.2.3 Tuning the Calabi-Yau condition

As pointed out in [18], in the absence of worldsheet instantons and for ∂αA⁡(Z)=0\partial_{\alpha}A(Z)=0, eq. (80) reduces to:

i​bα=Wgc​kα​(Z,Z¯)≠0.{\rm i}\,b_{\alpha}=W_{\rm gc}\,k_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})\neq 0\,. (92)

This induces a (2,1)(2,1)-component of HH (harmonic) that should vanish according to Strominger’s analysis [20]. However from (84), one may speculate that the CY condition can be preserved by envisaging a situation where one tunes the flux quanta such that bα=0b_{\alpha}=0 ∀α=1,…,hhol1,2\forall\alpha=1,...,h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} corresponding to H2,1=0H^{2,1}=0. The complex structure moduli would then be fixed by:

DZαW=0⇔WwiWgc=−1−∂αA⁡(Z)A⁡(Z)​kα​(Z,Z¯)1−∂αB⁡(Z)B⁡(Z)​kα​(Z,Z¯).D_{Z^{\alpha}}W=0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\frac{W_{\rm wi}}{W_{\rm gc}}=-\frac{1-\frac{\partial_{\alpha}A(Z)}{A(Z)k_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})}}{1-\frac{\partial_{\alpha}B(Z)}{B(Z)k_{\alpha}(Z,\bar{Z})}}\,. (93)

However now we have 4​hhol1,24\,h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} real equations determining 2​hhol1,22\,h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} real complex structure moduli. Obviously the system has no solution unless we scan over the integer fluxes. However there are only 2​h1,2+22\,h^{1,2}+2 integer fluxes. Thus we have only the freedom to scan over Q=2​(h1,2−hhol1,2+1)Q=2\left(h^{1,2}-h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}+1\right) integers while all 2​hhol1,22\,h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} real complex structure moduli as well as all but QQ of the integers (i.e. 2​hhol1,22\,h^{1,2}_{\rm hol} of them) must emerge as solutions to these non-linear equations. Thus we do not think that it is possible to have bα=0b_{\alpha}=0 in the presence of these non-perturbative terms. However, this condition emerges only on demanding a supersymmetric solution to the classical 10D equations, and so our 4D analysis cannot be expected to satisfy these classical conditions once non-perturbative effects are included.

3.3 Flux vacua counting

Let us clarify here a crucial difference between type IIB and heterotic string theory regarding complex structure stabilisation with three-form flux. The F-term equations (80) comprise 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} conditions for 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} real variables (setting now hhol1,2=h1,2h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=h^{1,2} for ease of comparison with type IIB). A non-trivial HH-flux yields exactly 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} independent flux quanta (up to the two related to the overall scaling of Ω⁡(Z)\Omega(Z)) generically supplying the non-linear system of h1,2h^{1,2} complex F-term conditions for the 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} complex structure moduli. However, the existence of a finite number of isolated solutions for such non-linear systems with as many equations as variables (rendering the system ‘well behaved’) is not guaranteed. One expects therefore that most of the available freedom of choice among the 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} HH-fluxes is used up to find a relatively small number of isolated solutions for the complex structure moduli where all of them sit safely in the regime of large complex structure. Generically, this precludes the possibility of using the HH-flux discretuum for tuning a very small VEV of WfluxW_{\rm flux}.

Note that this is different in the type IIB context. There, the availability of RR three-form flux F3F_{3} supplies an additional set of 2​h2,12\,h^{2,1} fluxes for an overall discretuum made up from 4​h1,24\,h^{1,2} fluxes. We have therefore an additional set of 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} discrete parameters available for tuning WfluxW_{\rm flux} while keeping a given well-behaved complex structure moduli vacuum. Consequently, after having used 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} flux parameters to construct a viable complex structure vacuum, we can use the additional 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} flux quanta to construct a ‘discrete 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2}-parameter family’ of complex structure vacua, which allows for exponential tuning of WfluxW_{\rm flux}.

Finally we note that in the heterotic case the unavailability of any additional freedom in the flux choice after fixing the ZZ-moduli, means that we have to depend on the far more restricted choices that are available in the solution space of the complex structure moduli. As mentioned before, one needs to scan over the HH flux integers in order to find 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} acceptable (i.e. in the geometric regime) real solutions to the 2​h1,22\,h^{1,2} non-linear equations DZα​W=0D_{Z^{\alpha}}W=0. The size of the solution set that we get is likely to be much smaller than the size of the original set of flux integers. Thus even if we had started with, let us say, h1,2=𝒪⁡(100)h^{1,2}=\mathcal{O}(100) and let each flux scan over 1 to 10, the number of acceptable fluxes are likely to be far smaller than what is required to tune the cosmological constant. It should also be emphasised here that the only source of tuning that is available after all the low-energy contributions to the vacuum energy are included, has to come from these fluxes.

4 Supersymmetry breaking vacua

In this section we shall show the existence of new Minkowski vacua with spontaneous supersymmetry breaking along the Kähler moduli directions. The strategy is to perform moduli stabilisation in two steps as follows:

  • •

    Step 1: Fix at leading order some of the moduli supersymmetrically (all the hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0 complex structure moduli, the dilaton and some Kähler moduli) at a high scale.

  • •

    Step 2: Stabilise the remaining light moduli at a lower scale breaking supersymmetry mainly along the Kähler directions by the inclusion of α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections to the Kähler potential in a way similar to type IIB.

In subsection 4.1 we shall consider the contributions to the scalar potential generated by fluxes, non-perturbative effects and threshold corrections showing that there exist no supersymmetry breaking minimum which lies in the regime of validity of the effective field theory. However, in subsection 4.2 we shall describe how this situation improves by the inclusion of α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections to the Kähler potential which yield trustworthy Minkowski vacua (see subsection 4.3) where supersymmetry is spontaneously broken by the F-terms of the Kähler moduli.1313 13 See [56] for another attempt to fix the heterotic moduli via the inclusion of α′\alpha^{\prime} effects. In subsection 4.4 we shall explain what is the rôle played by D-terms in our stabilisation procedure. Let us finally stress that this new procedure to obtain supersymmetry breaking vacua is completely orthogonal to the way the complex structure moduli are fixed, and so our results apply also to the case with hhol1,2=0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}=0 where there is no need to turn on quantised background fluxes to fix the ZZ-moduli.

4.1 Fluxes, non-perturbative effects and threshold corrections

In this section we shall derive the general expression for the scalar potential including fluxes, non-perturbative effects (both gaugino condensation and world-sheet instantons) and threshold corrections for a CY three-fold whose volume is given by:

𝒱=kb​tb3−ks​ts3.{\cal V}=k_{b}t_{b}^{3}-k_{s}t_{s}^{3}\,. (94)

The superpotential and the Kähler potential look like (neglecting a possible ZZ-dependence of AA and BB and setting for simplicity βs=0\beta_{s}=0):

W\displaystyle W =\displaystyle= Wflux​(Z)+A​e−λ⁡(S−βb2​Tb)+B​e−μ​Ts,\displaystyle W_{\rm flux}(Z)+A\,e^{-\lambda\left(S-\frac{\beta_{b}}{2}\,T_{b}\right)}+B\,e^{-\mu\,T_{s}}\,, (95)
K\displaystyle K =\displaystyle= −ln⁡𝒱−ln⁡(S+S¯)+Kcs​(Z,Z¯).\displaystyle-\ln{\cal V}-\ln\left(S+\bar{S}\right)+K_{\rm cs}(Z,\bar{Z})\,. (96)

Performing the following field redefinition:

Φ≡S−βb2​Tb,\Phi\equiv S-\frac{\beta_{b}}{2}\,T_{b}\,, (97)

    γs≤|cb|​ks1/3⇒δ​x≤ks1/3​ts𝒱1/3≃ϵs1/3≪1.\gamma_{s}\leq|c_{b}|k_{s}^{1/3}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\delta\,x\leq\frac{k_{s}^{1/3}t_{s}}{{\cal V}^{1/3}}\simeq\epsilon_{s}^{1/3}\ll 1\,. (125)

    Therefore the term in (123) proportional to |cb||c_{b}| has always a positive sign.

    If the condition |c|/ts3≪1|c|/t_{s}^{3}\ll 1 is not satisfied, there is no minimum for realistic values of the underlying parameters. In fact, in this case the term proportional to |C||C| is always sub-leading with respect to the term proportional to cbc_{b} since for c≥0c\geq 0:

    R≡|C|​x3|cb|​𝒱1/3≤(1+1+cts3)​ts3c​ϵs1/3x≪(1+1+cts3)​ts3c,R\equiv\frac{|C|\,x^{3}}{|c_{b}|\,{\cal V}^{1/3}}\leq\left(1+\sqrt{1+\frac{c}{t_{s}^{3}}}\right)\frac{t_{s}^{3}}{c}\frac{\epsilon_{s}^{1/3}}{x}\ll\left(1+\sqrt{1+\frac{c}{t_{s}^{3}}}\right)\frac{t_{s}^{3}}{c}\,, (126)

showing that if we want to have a Minkowski minimum A1A_{1} has to be positive, i.e. βb>0\beta_{b}>0.

4.3 Minkowski solutions

Let us first define our use of the term ‘Minkowski solutions’. Owing to the lack of tuning freedom in the heterotic three-form flux superpotential, achieving vacua with exponentially small vacuum energy is a real challenge. Thus we shall use the terminology ‘Minkowski vacuum’ to refer to a vacuum with a cosmological constant suppressed by at least a 1-loop factor 1/(8​π2)≃0.011/(8\pi^{2})\simeq 0.01 compared to the height of the barrier in the scalar potential (of order m3/22​MP2m_{3/2}^{2}M_{P}^{2}) which protects the TT-moduli from run-away.

The solutions depend on seven underlying parameters: ks,kb,βb,|B|,|cb|,|κ|k_{s},k_{b},\beta_{b},|B|,|c_{b}|,|\kappa| and ξ\xi. We do not consider |W0eff||W_{0}^{\rm eff}| as a free variable at this stage since we fix its value at |W0eff|=0.06|W_{0}^{\rm eff}|=0.06 by the phenomenological requirement of obtaining the right GUT coupling corresponding to ⟨s⟩≃⟨ϕ⟩≃2\langle s\rangle\simeq\langle\phi\rangle\simeq 2. Let us now describe a strategy to find the values of these underlying parameters which give Minkowski vacua for desired values of the moduli and within the regime of validity of all our approximations.

  1. 1.

    Choose the desired values for 𝒱{\cal V} and tst_{s} (so fixing the value of x=2​π​tsx=2\pi\,t_{s}). Then work out the value of |B||B| as a function of ksk_{s} from (113).

  2. 2.

    Choose the desired value of tbt_{b} and work out the value of kbk_{b} as a function of ksk_{s} from (94).

  3. 3.

    Determine |cb||c_{b}| as a function of ks,ξk_{s},\xi and |κ||\kappa| from (135).

  4. 4.

    Derive the value of βb\beta_{b} as a function of ks,ξk_{s},\xi and |κ||\kappa| from (137).

  5. 5.

    Choose the values of ks,ξk_{s},\xi and |κ||\kappa| so that all our approximations are under control, i.e. ϵϕ\epsilon_{\phi} defined in (101) satisfies ϵϕ≪1\epsilon_{\phi}\ll 1, ϵs\epsilon_{s} defined in (102) gives ϵs≪1\epsilon_{s}\ll 1, δ\delta defined in (124) satisfies δ≪1\delta\ll 1 and ϵα′≡ξ/(2​𝒱)≪1\epsilon_{\alpha^{\prime}}\equiv\xi/(2{\cal V})\ll 1. These values of ks,ξk_{s},\xi and |κ||\kappa| then give the values of kb,|B|,|cb|k_{b},|B|,|c_{b}| and βb\beta_{b} knowing that this Minkowski vacuum is fully consistent.

As an illustrative example, following this procedure we found a Minkowski vacuum (see Fig. 2) located at:

⟨ϕ⟩≃⟨s⟩=2,⟨𝒱⟩=20,⟨tb⟩≃5,⟨ts⟩=1.5,\langle\phi\rangle\simeq\langle s\rangle=2\,,\qquad\langle{\cal V}\rangle=20\,,\qquad\langle t_{b}\rangle\simeq 5\,,\qquad\langle t_{s}\rangle=1.5\,, (138)

for the following choice of the microscopic parameters:

kb\displaystyle k_{b} =\displaystyle= ks=1/6,βb≃0.035,|W0eff|=0.06,cb=0.75,cs=−0.75,\displaystyle k_{s}=1/6\,,\quad\beta_{b}\simeq 0.035\,,\quad|W_{0}^{\rm eff}|=0.06\,,\quad c_{b}=0.75\,,\quad c_{s}=-0.75\,,
B\displaystyle B ≃\displaystyle\simeq 3,ξ≃1.49,μ=2​π⇒γs≃0.41,κ=0.\displaystyle 3\,,\quad\xi\simeq 1.49\,,\quad\mu=2\pi\quad\Rightarrow\quad\gamma_{s}\simeq 0.41\,,\quad\kappa=0\,. (139)

Note that one can get dS or AdS solutions by varying βb\beta_{b} either above or below its benchmark value. Moreover, our approximations are under control since:

ϵϕ≃0.043,ϵs≃0.027,ϵα′≃0.037,δ≃0.032.\epsilon_{\phi}\simeq 0.043\,,\qquad\epsilon_{s}\simeq 0.027\,,\qquad\epsilon_{\alpha^{\prime}}\simeq 0.037\,,\qquad\delta\simeq 0.032\,. (140)

We stress that at the minimum these four quantities are all of the same size: ϵϕ≃ϵs≃ϵα′≃δ\epsilon_{\phi}\simeq\epsilon_{s}\simeq\epsilon_{\alpha^{\prime}}\simeq\delta. This has to be the case since they weight the relative strengths of loops, non-perturbative and higher derivative effects which all compete to give a minimum.

Moreover, we point out that there seem to be problems with the α′\alpha^{\prime} expansion since we managed to obtain a minimum by tuning the underlying parameters in order to have the 𝒪⁡(α′2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}) term of the same order of magnitude of the 𝒪⁡(α′3)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 3}) term, and so higher order α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections might not be negligible.

However this might not be a problem if at least one of the following is valid:

  • •

    The 𝒪⁡(α′2)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 2}) corrections could be eliminated by a proper redefinition of the moduli.

  • •

    The coefficients of higher order α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections are not tuned larger than unity, resulting in a α′\alpha^{\prime} expansion which is under control. In fact, the α′\alpha^{\prime} expansion parameter is of order q𝒱−1/3q{\cal V}^{-1/3} with qq an unknown coefficient. Thus 𝒪⁡(α′4)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime 4}) contributions to the scalar potential can be estimated as:

    Vα′4Vα′3≃2​q3​ξ​𝒱1/3≃0.16forq=1.\frac{V_{\alpha^{\prime 4}}}{V_{\alpha^{\prime 3}}}\simeq\frac{2q}{3\xi{\cal V}^{1/3}}\simeq 0.16\qquad\text{for}\qquad q=1\,. (141)

4.4 D-term potential

So far only F-terms have been taken into account. This could be consistent since moduli-dependent D-terms might not be present in the absence of anomalous U⁡(1)U(1)s, or they might be cancelled by giving suitable VEVs to charged matter fields.

However let us see how D-terms might change the previous picture in the presence of anomalous U⁡(1)U(1)s but without introducing charged matter fields. Because of the U⁡(1)U(1)-invariance of the superpotential (98), both Φ\Phi and TsT_{s} have to be neutral. Therefore the only field which can be charged under an anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) is TbT_{b} with qTb=4​c1b​(ℒ)≠0q_{T_{b}}=4\,c_{1}^{b}(\mathcal{L})\neq 0. From (32), this induces an FI-term of the form:

ξ=−qTb​Kb=qTb​(kb𝒱)1/3,\xi=-\,q_{T_{b}}K_{b}=q_{T_{b}}\left(\frac{k_{b}}{{\cal V}}\right)^{1/3}\,, (142)

which gives the following D-term potential:

VD=ξ2Re⁡(f)≃p𝒱2/3withp≡qTb2​kb2/3ϕ.V_{D}=\frac{\xi^{2}}{{\rm Re}(f)}\simeq\frac{p}{{\cal V}^{2/3}}\qquad\text{with}\qquad p\equiv\frac{q_{T_{b}}^{2}\,k_{b}^{2/3}}{\phi}\,. (143)

This term has the same volume scaling as the first term in (130) which is the contribution coming from threshold effects. However the ratio between these two terms scales as:

VthresholdVD=ϵϕ𝒱1/3​|W0eff|2qTb2​kb2/3≪1,\frac{V_{\rm threshold}}{V_{D}}=\frac{\epsilon_{\phi}}{{\cal V}^{1/3}}\,\frac{|W_{0}^{\rm eff}|^{2}}{q_{T_{b}}^{2}\,k_{b}^{2/3}}\ll 1\,, (144)

for ϵϕ≪1\epsilon_{\phi}\ll 1 and qTb∼𝒪⁡(1)q_{T_{b}}\sim\mathcal{O}(1). As an illustrative example, our explicit parameter choice would give Vthreshold/VD≃2⋅10−4​qTb−2V_{\rm threshold}/V_{D}\simeq 2\cdot 10^{-4}\,q_{T_{b}}^{-2}, showing that VDV_{D} is always dominant with respect to the F-term potential (130). In this case, VDV_{D} would give a run-away for the volume direction and destroy our moduli stabilisation scenario.

As we have already pointed out, this might not be the case if there are no anomalous U⁡(1)U(1)s or if the FI-term is cancelled by a matter field VEV. There is however another way-out to this D-term problem which relies on the possibility to fix all the moduli charged under anomalous U⁡(1)U(1)s in a completely supersymmetric way, so ensuring the vanishing of the D-term potential. This requires qTb=0q_{T_{b}}=0 and the addition of a third Kähler modulus TcT_{c} which is charged under an anomalous U⁡(1)U(1): qTc≠0q_{T_{c}}\neq 0. Let us describe this situation in the next subsection.

4.4.1 D + F-term stabilisation

The Kähler and superpotential now read:

W\displaystyle W =\displaystyle= Wflux​(Z)+A​e−λ⁡(Φ−βc2​Tc)+B​e−μ​Ts,\displaystyle W_{\rm flux}(Z)+A\,e^{-\lambda\left(\Phi-\frac{\beta_{c}}{2}\,T_{c}\right)}+B\,e^{-\mu\,T_{s}}\,, (145)
K\displaystyle K =\displaystyle= −ln⁡𝒱~−ln⁡[Φ+Φ¯+βb2​(Tb+T¯b)]+Kcs​(Z),\displaystyle-\ln\tilde{{\cal V}}-\ln\left[\Phi+\bar{\Phi}+\frac{\beta_{b}}{2}\left(T_{b}+\bar{T}_{b}\right)\right]+K_{\rm cs}(Z)\,, (146)

with

𝒱~=𝒱−kc​tc3=kb​tb3−ks​ts3−kc​tc3.\tilde{{\cal V}}={\cal V}-k_{c}t_{c}^{3}=k_{b}t_{b}^{3}-k_{s}t_{s}^{3}-k_{c}t_{c}^{3}\,. (147)

Note that now Φ\Phi has to get charged under an anomalous U⁡(1)U(1) so that the hidden sector gauge kinetic function fhid=Φ−βc2​Tcf_{\rm hid}=\Phi-\frac{\beta_{c}}{2}\,T_{c} becomes gauge invariant. In particular we will have qΦ=βc2​qTcq_{\Phi}=\frac{\beta_{c}}{2}\,q_{T_{c}}. From (32), the FI-term looks like:

ξ=−qΦ​DΦ​WW−qTc​DTc​WW,\xi=-q_{\Phi}\,\frac{D_{\Phi}W}{W}-q_{T_{c}}\,\frac{D_{T_{c}}W}{W}\,, (148)

implying that VD=0V_{D}=0 if both Φ\Phi and TcT_{c} are fixed supersymmetrically. However we have already seen that if all the Kähler moduli are fixed supersymmetrically via threshold effects, then perturbation theory breaks down in the hidden sector and the visible sector gauge kinetic function becomes negative. A way-out proposed in section 3.2.2 was to include worldsheet instantons but, given that we want to break supersymmetry at leading order along TbT_{b} and TsT_{s}, in order to follow this possibility we should include a fourth modulus with worldsheet instantons. Thus this case does not look very appealing since it requires at least four moduli.

A simpler solution can be found by noticing that the problems with Re⁡(fhid1−loop)>Re⁡(fhidtree){\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm hid}^{\rm 1-loop}\right)>\,{\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm hid}^{\rm tree}\right) and Re⁡(fvis)<0{\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm vis}\right)<0 could be avoided if only some but not all of the Kähler moduli are fixed supersymmetrically by threshold effects. We shall now prove that this is indeed the case if the TT-moduli fixed in this way are blow-up modes like tct_{c}. In fact, the solution to DTc​W=0D_{T_{c}}W=0 gives:

βc=−s𝒱​kc​j​k​tj​tk=−6​s𝒱​kc​tc2.\beta_{c}=-\frac{s}{{\cal V}}\,k_{cjk}t_{j}t_{k}=-\frac{6\,s}{{\cal V}}\,k_{c}t_{c}^{2}\,. (149)

This result, in turn, gives hidden and visible sector gauge kinetic functions of the form:

Re⁡(fhid1−loop)Re⁡(fhidtree)=−βb​tb2​s−βc​tc2​s=−ϵϕ+3​kc​tc3𝒱=−ϵϕ+3​ϵs≪1,\frac{{\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm hid}^{\rm 1-loop}\right)}{{\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm hid}^{\rm tree}\right)}=-\frac{\beta_{b}t_{b}}{2s}-\frac{\beta_{c}t_{c}}{2s}=-\epsilon_{\phi}+3\,\frac{k_{c}\,t_{c}^{3}}{{\cal V}}=-\epsilon_{\phi}+3\epsilon_{s}\ll 1\,,

and:

Re⁡(fvis)=s⁡(1+βb​tb2​s+βc​tc2​c)=s⁡(1+ϵϕ−3​kc​tc3𝒱)=s⁡(1+ϵϕ−3​ϵs)≃s>0.{\rm Re}\left(f_{\rm vis}\right)=s\left(1+\frac{\beta_{b}t_{b}}{2s}+\frac{\beta_{c}t_{c}}{2c}\right)=s\left(1+\epsilon_{\phi}-3\,\frac{k_{c}t_{c}^{3}}{{\cal V}}\right)=s\left(1+\epsilon_{\phi}-3\,\epsilon_{s}\right)\simeq s>0\,.

5 Moduli mass spectrum, supersymmetry breaking and soft terms

Expanding the effective field theory around the vacua found in the previous section, we can derive the moduli mass spectrum which turns out to be (see (122) and (124) for the definitions of xx and δ\delta):

mts\displaystyle m_{t_{s}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq mas≃m3/2​x,\displaystyle m_{a_{s}}\simeq m_{3/2}\,x\,,
mZα\displaystyle m_{Z^{\alpha}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq mΦ≃m3/2,\displaystyle m_{\Phi}\simeq m_{3/2}\,,
mtb\displaystyle m_{t_{b}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq m3/2​δ,\displaystyle m_{3/2}\,\delta\,,
mab\displaystyle m_{a_{b}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq 0.\displaystyle 0\,. (150)

Note that in the absence of TbT_{b}-dependent worldsheet instantons which would give aba_{b} a mass of order mab≃MP​e−μ​tb≃10m_{a_{b}}\simeq M_{P}\,e^{-\mu\,t_{b}}\simeq 10 TeV for tb≃5t_{b}\simeq 5, this axion might be a good QCD axion candidate since it could remain a flat direction until standard QCD non-perturbative effects give it a tiny mass.

Moreover, the stabilisation procedure described in the previous sections leads to vacua which break supersymmetry spontaneously mainly along the Kähler moduli directions. In fact, from the general expression of the F-terms and the gravitino mass:

Fi=eK/2​Ki​j¯​Dj¯​W¯andm3/2=eK/2​|W|≃|W0eff|𝒱1/2,F^{i}=e^{K/2}K^{i\bar{j}}D_{\bar{j}}\bar{W}\qquad\text{and}\qquad m_{3/2}=e^{K/2}|W|\simeq\frac{|W_{0}^{\rm eff}|}{{\cal V}^{1/2}}\,, (151)

we find that the Kähler moduli F-terms read:

FTbtb=−2​m3/2andFTsts≃m3/2x.\frac{F^{T_{b}}}{t_{b}}=-2\,m_{3/2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{F^{T_{s}}}{t_{s}}\simeq\frac{m_{3/2}}{x}\,. (152)

On the other hand, the dilaton and the complex structure moduli are fixed supersymmetrically at leading order. However, due to the fact that the prefactor of worldsheet instantons and α′\alpha^{\prime} effects are expected to depend on these moduli, they would also break supersymmetry at sub-leading order developing F-terms whose magnitude can be estimated as:1414 14 Assuming that there are no cancellations from shifts of the minimum due to sub-leading corrections.

DZα,Φ​W≃DZα,Φ​Wwi≃δ​|W0eff|⇒FZα,Φ≃δ​m3/2.D_{Z^{\alpha},\Phi}W\simeq D_{Z^{\alpha},\Phi}W_{\rm wi}\simeq\delta\,|W_{0}^{\rm eff}|\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad F^{Z^{\alpha},\Phi}\simeq\delta\,m_{3/2}\,. (153)

Thus we can see that supersymmetry is mainly broken along the tbt_{b}-direction since:

FTbm3/2≃tb≫FTsm3/2≃tsx≫FZα,Φm3/2≃δ.\frac{F^{T_{b}}}{m_{3/2}}\simeq t_{b}\gg\frac{F^{T_{s}}}{m_{3/2}}\simeq\frac{t_{s}}{x}\gg\frac{F^{Z^{\alpha},\Phi}}{m_{3/2}}\simeq\delta\,. (154)

The goldstino is therefore mainly the TbT_{b}-modulino which is eaten up by the gravitino in the super-Higgs mechanism.

Soft supersymmetry breaking terms are generated in the visible sector via tree-level gravitational interactions due to moduli mediation. Let us now derive their expressions:

  • •

    Gaugino masses: Their canonically normalised expression is given by:

    M1/2=12​R​e​(fvis)​Fi​∂ifvis≃FΦ2​ϕ+δ​FTbtb≃δ​m3/2,M_{1/2}=\frac{1}{2{\rm Re}(f_{\rm vis})}\,F^{i}\partial_{i}f_{\rm vis}\simeq\frac{F^{\Phi}}{2\phi}+\delta\,\frac{F^{T_{b}}}{t_{b}}\simeq\delta\,m_{3/2}\,, (155)

    showing that the gaugino masses are suppressed with respect to the gravitino mass by a factor of order δ≃0.03\delta\simeq 0.03.

  • •

    Scalar masses: The canonically normalised scalar masses generated by gravity mediation read:

    m0,α2=m3/22−Fi​F¯j¯​∂i∂j¯ln⁡K~α,m_{0,\,\alpha}^{2}=m_{3/2}^{2}-F^{i}\bar{F}^{\bar{j}}\partial_{i}\partial_{\bar{j}}\ln\tilde{K}_{\alpha}\,, (156)

    where K~α\tilde{K}_{\alpha} is the Kähler metric for matter fields which we assumed to be diagonal. K~α\tilde{K}_{\alpha} is generically a function of all the moduli but we shall neglect its dependence on the dilaton and the complex structure moduli since they give only a sub-leading contribution to supersymmetry breaking. Hence we shall consider a Kähler metric for matter fields of the form K~α≃ts−ns​tb−nb\tilde{K}_{\alpha}\simeq t_{s}^{-n_{s}}\,t_{b}^{-n_{b}}, where nsn_{s} and nbn_{b} are the so-called modular weights. In the type IIB set-up, it is possible to determine the value of nbn_{b} by requiring physical Yukawa couplings which do not depend on the large cycle due to the localisation of the visible sector on one of the small cycles [57]. However, in the heterotic framework the situation is different. For instance, in CY compactifications close to the orbifold point the visible sector typically is constructed from split multiplets which partially live in the bulk and partially arise as twisted sector states localised at orbifold fixed points. The value of the modular weights for the different matter fields is then determined by the requirements of modular invariance. Hence, they cannot be constrained by using an argument similar to the one in [57]. We shall therefore leave them as undetermined parameters. The scalar masses turn out to be:

    m02=m3/22​(1−nb−ns4​x2),m_{0}^{2}=m_{3/2}^{2}\left(1-n_{b}-\frac{n_{s}}{4x^{2}}\right)\,, (157)

    showing that for x≫1x\gg 1, the modular weight nbn_{b} has to be nb≤1n_{b}\leq 1 in order to avoid tachyonic squarks and sleptons. If nb=1n_{b}=1, one has a leading order cancellation in the scalar masses which therefore get generated by the F-terms of the small cycle tst_{s} even if FTs≪FTbF^{T_{s}}\ll F^{T_{b}} (in this case one would need ns<0n_{s}<0). This is indeed the case in type IIB models because of the no-scale structure [58]. Given that the no-scale cancellation holds in the heterotic case as well, we expect a similar cancellation to occur in our case, i.e. nb=1n_{b}=1, with possibly the exception of twisted matter fields at orbifold fixed points, i.e. nb<1n_{b}<1 for twisted states.

  • •

    A-terms: The canonically normalised A-terms look like:

    Aα​β​γ=Fi​[Ki+∂iln⁡Yα​β​γ−∂iln⁡(K~α​K~β​K~γ)],A_{\alpha\beta\gamma}=F^{i}\left[K_{i}+\partial_{i}\ln Y_{\alpha\beta\gamma}-\partial_{i}\ln\left(\tilde{K}_{\alpha}\tilde{K}_{\beta}\tilde{K}_{\gamma}\right)\right]\,, (158)

    where Yα​β​γY_{\alpha\beta\gamma} are the canonically unnormalised Yukawa couplings which can in principle depend on all the moduli. Similarly to the Kähler metric for matter fields, we introduce two modular weights, pbp_{b} and psp_{s}, and we write the Yukawa couplings as Yα​β​γ≃tb−pb​ts−psY_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\simeq t_{b}^{-p_{b}}\,t_{s}^{-p_{s}}. Thus the A-terms take the form:

    Aα​β​γ=3​m3/2​(1+pb−nb+ps2​x−ns2​x−δ3​x).A_{\alpha\beta\gamma}=3m_{3/2}\left(1+p_{b}-n_{b}+\frac{p_{s}}{2x}-\frac{n_{s}}{2x}-\frac{\delta}{3x}\right)\,. (159)

    In the type IIB case, there is again a leading order cancellation (since nb=1n_{b}=1 and pb=0p_{b}=0 given that the Yukawa couplings do not depend on the Kähler moduli due to the axionic shift-symmetry and the holomorphicity of WW) which is again due to the no-scale structure [58]. Similarly to the scalar masses, we expect this leading order cancellation also in the heterotic case for matter fields living in the bulk.

  • •

    μ\mu and Bμ\mu-term: The μ\mu-term can be generated by a standard Giudice-Masiero term in the Kähler potential K⊃K~​(ts,tb)​Hu​HdK\supset\tilde{K}(t_{s},t_{b})H_{u}H_{d} which gives again μ≃m3/2\mu\simeq m_{3/2} and B​μ≃m3/22B\mu\simeq m_{3/2}^{2}.

Summarising, we obtained a very specific pattern of soft terms with scalars heavier than the gauginos and universal A-terms and μ\mu/B​μB\mu-term of the order the gravitino mass:

m0≃Aα​β​γ≃μ≃B≃m3/2≫M1/2≃δ​m3/2.m_{0}\simeq A_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\simeq\mu\simeq B\simeq m_{3/2}\gg M_{1/2}\simeq\delta\,m_{3/2}\,. (160)

The soft masses scale with m3/2m_{3/2} and do not depend on the mechanism which stabilises the complex structure and bundle moduli. Hence one can obtain TeV-scale supersymmetry by considering either smooth CY models where all the complex structure moduli are fixed by the holomorphicity of the gauge bundle or orbifold constructions with a small number of untwisted ZZ-moduli (or better with no untwisted ZZ-moduli at all as in the case of some non-Abelian orbifolds). On general Calabi-Yau manifolds, we expect the soft mass scale to be of order m3/2∼MGUTm_{3/2}\sim M_{\rm{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}} due the fact that in the heterotic string there is not enough freedom to tune the flux superpotential below values of 𝒪⁡(0.1−0.01)\mathcal{O}(0.1-0.01).

6 Anisotropic solutions

In this section we shall show how to generalise the previous results to obtain anisotropic compactifications with 2 large and 4 small extra dimensions which allow for a right value of the GUT scale.1515 15 For anisotropic solutions in the type IIB case for the same kind of fibred CY manifolds see [59, 60, 61]. For this purpose, we shall focus on CY three-folds whose volume is [62]:

𝒱=kb​tb​tf2−ks​ts3.{\cal V}=k_{b}t_{b}t_{f}^{2}-k_{s}t_{s}^{3}\,. (161)

This CY admits a 4D K3 or T4T^{4} divisor of volume tf2t_{f}^{2} fibered over a 2D ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} base of volume tbt_{b} with an additional del Pezzo divisor of size ts2t_{s}^{2}. We shall now show how to fix the moduli dynamically in the anisotropic region tb≫tf∼tst_{b}\gg t_{f}\sim t_{s}. We shall consider a hidden sector gauge kinetic function of the form:

fhid=S−βb2​Tb−βf2​Tf≡Φ,withβs=0.f_{\rm hid}=S-\frac{\beta_{b}}{2}\,T_{b}-\frac{\beta_{f}}{2}\,T_{f}\equiv\Phi\,,\qquad\text{with}\qquad\beta_{s}=0\,. (162)

The superpotential looks exactly as the one in (98) whereas the Kähler potential reads:

K=−ln⁡𝒱−ln⁡[Φ+Φ¯+βb2​(Tb+T¯b)+βf2​(Tf+T¯f)]+Kcs​(Z).K=-\ln{\cal V}-\ln\left[\Phi+\bar{\Phi}+\frac{\beta_{b}}{2}\left(T_{b}+\bar{T}_{b}\right)+\frac{\beta_{f}}{2}\left(T_{f}+\bar{T}_{f}\right)\right]+K_{\rm cs}(Z)\,. (163)

Focusing on the limit where 1-loop effects are suppressed with respect to the tree-level expression of the gauge kinetic function:

ϵb≡βb​tb2​ϕ≪1andϵf≡βf​tf2​ϕ≪1,\epsilon_{b}\equiv\frac{\beta_{b}\,t_{b}}{2\phi}\ll 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\epsilon_{f}\equiv\frac{\beta_{f}\,t_{f}}{2\phi}\ll 1\,, (164)

the dilaton is again fixed at leading order by requiring DΦ​W=0D_{\Phi}W=0. On the other hand the Kähler moduli develop a subdominant potential via non-perturbative contributions, α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections and threshold effects which break the no-scale structure as:

∑TKi​j¯​Ki​Kj¯−3=2​(ϵb+ϵf)+𝒪⁡(ϵ2).\sum_{T}K^{i\bar{j}}K_{i}K_{\bar{j}}-3=2\left(\epsilon_{b}+\epsilon_{f}\right)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})\,. (165)

The scalar potential has therefore the same expression as (109) but with a different coefficient A1A_{1} which is now moduli-dependent and looks like:

A1​(𝒱,tf)=𝒱2/32​⟨ϕ⟩​(βbkb​tf2+βf​tf𝒱),A_{1}({\cal V},t_{f})=\frac{{\cal V}^{2/3}}{2\langle\phi\rangle}\left(\frac{\beta_{b}}{k_{b}t_{f}^{2}}+\frac{\beta_{f}\,t_{f}}{{\cal V}}\right)\,, (166)

where we have traded tbt_{b} for 𝒱{\cal V}. This is the only term which depends on tft_{f} since the rest of the potential depends just on 𝒱{\cal V} and tst_{s}. Hence we can fix tft_{f} just minimising A1​(𝒱,tf)A_{1}({\cal V},t_{f}) obtaining:

tf=(2​βbkb​βf)1/3𝒱1/3⇔tf=2​βbβftb.t_{f}=\left(\frac{2\beta_{b}}{k_{b}\beta_{f}}\right)^{1/3}{\cal V}^{1/3}\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad t_{f}=\frac{2\beta_{b}}{\beta_{f}}\,t_{b}\,. (167)

Substituting this result in (166) we find that A1A_{1} becomes:

A1=3​βb2​⟨ϕ⟩​kb1/3​(βf2​βb)2/3,A_{1}=\frac{3\beta_{b}}{2\langle\phi\rangle k_{b}^{1/3}}\left(\frac{\beta_{f}}{2\beta_{b}}\right)^{2/3}\,, (168)

which is not moduli-dependent anymore and takes a form very similar to the one in (110). We can therefore follow the same stabilisation procedure described in the previous sections but now with the additional relation (167) which, allowing the moderate tuning βf≃20​βb\beta_{f}\simeq 20\,\beta_{b}, would give an anisotropic solution with tb≃10​tft_{b}\simeq 10\,t_{f}. For example for 𝒱≃20{\cal V}\simeq 20 and kb=1/2k_{b}=1/2, one would obtain tb≃16≫tf≃1.6t_{b}\simeq 16\gg t_{f}\simeq 1.6.

We finally mention that this kind of fibred CY manifolds have been successfully used in type IIB for deriving inflationary models from string theory where the inflaton is the Kähler modulus controlling the volume of the fibre [63]. It would be very interesting to investigate if similar cosmological applications could also be present in the heterotic case.

7 Conclusions

The heterotic string on a CY manifold (or its various limiting cases such as orbifolds and Gepner points) has been studied since the late eighties as a possible UV complete theory of gravity that can realise a unified version of the SM. In the last decade there has been much progress towards the goal of getting a realistic model with the correct spectrum. However the major problem in getting phenomenologically viable solutions for the heterotic string is that the gauge theory resides in the bulk, and so getting an acceptable model cannot be decoupled from the problem of moduli stabilisation. Unfortunately a complete and deep understanding of the mechanism which stabilises all the moduli in the heterotic string is still lacking.

In this paper we tried to perform a systematic analysis of all the effects which can develop a potential for the various moduli for the case of (0,2)(0,2)-compactifications which allow for MSSM-like model building and the generation of worldsheet instantons that are crucial effects to fix the Kähler moduli. According to the original Strominger’s analysis [20], these compactifications violate the Kähler condition d​J=0dJ=0 due to a non-zero HH-flux at 𝒪⁡(α′)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime}) since in the non-standard embedding the co-exact piece of the Chern-Simons term in HH does not cancel. We then considered solutions to the 10D equations of motion with constant dilaton and warp factor, corresponding to ‘special Hermitian manifolds’, which represent the smallest deviations from smooth CY manifolds at 𝒪⁡(α′)\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{\prime}) [39].

Let us summarise the various moduli stabilisation effects that we have taken into account:

  • •

    Holomorphicity of the gauge bundle, D-terms and higher order perturbative contributions to the superpotential: By demanding a supersymmetric gauge bundle, i.e. a gauge bundle which satisfies the Hermitian Yang-Mills equations, the combined space of complex structure and gauge bundle moduli reduces from a naive direct product to a ‘cross-structure’ [33, 34, 35, 36]. Therefore if the gauge bundle moduli are fixed at non-zero VEVs by D-terms combined with higher order perturbative contributions to the superpotential [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], the ZZ-moduli are automatically lifted. However, not all the complex structure moduli might get frozen by this mechanism since, in general, the sub-locus in complex structure moduli space where the gauge bundle is holomorphic turns out to have dimension hhol1,2>0h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}>0. Hence 0<hhol1,2<h1,20<h^{1,2}_{\rm hol}<h^{1,2} flat ZZ-moduli are generically left over.

  • •

    Fractional Chern-Simons invariants, gaugino condensation and threshold effects: The remaining flat ZZ-directions could be lifted by turning on quantised background three-form fluxes [17, 18, 19]. However we showed that, contrary to type IIB, this cannot be done having at the same time a vanishing VEV of the tree-level flux superpotential W0W_{0} since setting the F-terms of the ZZ-moduli to zero corresponds to setting the (1,2)(1,2)-component of the HH-flux to zero, while demanding W0=0W_{0}=0 implies that also the (3,0)(3,0)-piece of HH is vanishing. Hence, being real, the whole HH-flux has to be zero, resulting in the impossibility of fixing the remaining complex structure moduli. Thus one needs W0≠0W_{0}\neq 0 in order to fix the ZZ-moduli. However, due to the absence of Ramond-Ramond fluxes, it is hard to tune W0W_{0} small enough to balance the exponentially suppressed contribution from gaugino condensation which introduces an explicit dependence on the dilaton [11, 12, 13] unless one turns on fractional Chern-Simons invariants (i.e. discrete Wilson lines) [17]. In this way both the dilaton and the complex structure moduli can be stabilised supersymmetrically at non-perturbative level. The Kähler moduli could then be fixed by the inclusion of threshold corrections to the gauge kinetic function [21, 22].

  • •

    Worldsheet instantons: The supersymmetric minimum obtained by including threshold effects is not in the weak coupling regime where one can trust the effective field theory. This problem can be avoided by considering also the contribution of TT-dependent worldsheet instantons which can give rise to reliable supersymmetric AdS vacua [19].

  • •

    Higher derivative and loop corrections to the Kähler potential: The last effects to be taken into account are α′\alpha^{\prime} corrections to the Kähler potential [23, 24, 25], while string loop effects can be estimated to give rise to negligible contributions to the scalar potential [47, 48, 49]. These higher derivative corrections yield new stable vacua where supersymmetry is spontaneously broken by the stabilisation mechanism which induces non-zero F-terms for the Kähler moduli, in a way very similar to type IIB LARGE Volume Scenarios [26, 27]. These new vacua can be Minkowski due to the positive contribution from threshold effects. However, due to the lack of tuning freedom in W0W_{0}, it is very hard to achieve vacua with exponentially small vacuum energy. Thus we used the term ‘Minkowski vacua’ to refer to solutions with a cosmological constant suppressed by at least a loop factor with respect to the height of the barrier in the scalar potential which prevents the Kähler moduli to run-away to infinity. Moreover, this stabilisation mechanism allows for anisotropic compactifications with two extra dimensions which are much larger than the other four. In this way, the unification scale can be lowered down to the observed phenomenological value [28, 29], fitting very well with the picture of 6D orbifold GUTs [29, 30].

After showing the existence of this new kind of supersymmetry breaking vacua, we estimated the size of the soft terms generated by gravity mediation. Interestingly, they feature universal scalar masses, A-terms and μ/B​μ\mu/B\mu-term of 𝒪⁡(m3/2)\mathcal{O}(m_{3/2}) and suppressed gaugino masses at the %-level. Moreover, a potentially viable QCD axion candidate is given by the axionic partner of the ‘large’ 2-cycle modulus. However, due to the lack of tuning freedom in the flux superpotential W0≃𝒪⁡(0.1−0.01)W_{0}\simeq\mathcal{O}(0.1-0.01), the gravitino mass m3/2=W0​MP/2​Re​(S)​𝒱m_{3/2}=W_{0}M_{P}/\sqrt{2\rm{Re}(S){\cal V}} becomes of order MG​U​T≃1016M_{{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}}\simeq 10^{16} GeV for Re⁡(S)≃2\rm{Re}(S)\simeq 2 and 𝒱≃20{\cal V}\simeq 20. This is not a problem if one does not believe in the solution of the hierarchy problem based on low-energy supersymmetry, but it represents a generic prediction of weakly coupled heterotic compactifications on internal manifolds which are smooth CY three-folds up to α′\alpha^{\prime} effects.

However, our stabilisation procedure for the Kähler moduli that leads to spontaneous supersymmetry breaking, is completely independent on the supersymmetric mechanism which is used to fix the dilaton and the complex structure moduli. Hence, if one is instead interested in low-energy supersymmetry, our way to break supersymmetry along the Kähler moduli directions could still be used by focusing on different ways to freeze the SS- and ZZ-moduli:

  1. 1.

    In some particular examples all the complex structure moduli could be stabilised by the requirement of a holomorphic gauge bundle [33, 34, 35]. In this case one could have W0=0W_{0}=0 and an exponentially small superpotential, leading to a TeV-scale gravitino mass, could be generated by gaugino condensation.

  2. 2.

    In Abelian orbifold models the number of untwisted complex structure moduli is very small. There are also some non-Abelian orbifolds with no ZZ-moduli at all. Hence in this case it is rather likely that all the ZZ-moduli could be fixed by the holomorphicity of the gauge bundle once all the singlets are fixed at non-zero VEVs by cancelling FI-terms or by the effect of higher order terms in WW [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Again, m3/2m_{3/2} could then be lowered to the TeV-scale due to the exponential suppression coming from gaugino condensation [31, 32].

  3. 3.

    The flux superpotential could have enough tuning freedom in the presence of fluxes which are the equivalent of type IIB Ramond-Ramond fluxes. This is the case of non-complex manifolds with new geometric fluxes where the HH flux gets modified to ℋ=H+i​d​J\mathcal{H}=H+{\rm i}\,dJ [39, 41, 42, 43, 44].1616 16 See also [64].

We finally stress that, even if these models could give low-energy supersymmetry, the possibility to tune the cosmological constant to the observed value still remains a challenge, in particular in the cases without a large flux discretuum.

Appendix A Dimensional reduction of 10D heterotic action

The 10D heterotic supergravity action in string frame for energies below the mass of the first excited string state Ms=ℓs−1M_{s}=\ell_{s}^{-1} with ℓs=2​π​α′\ell_{s}=2\pi\sqrt{\alpha^{\prime}} contains bosonic terms of the form:

S\displaystyle S ⊃\displaystyle\supset 1(2​π)7​α′4​∫d10​x​−G​e−2​ϕ​(ℛ−α′4​Tr​F2)\displaystyle\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{7}\alpha^{\prime 4}}\int d^{10}x\sqrt{-G}\,e^{-2\phi}\left(\mathcal{R}-\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{4}{\rm Tr}F^{2}\right) (169)
=\displaystyle= M1082​∫d10​x​−G​e−2​ϕ​ℛ−12​g102​∫d10​x​−G​e−2​ϕ​Tr​F2.\displaystyle\frac{M_{\scriptscriptstyle 10}^{8}}{2}\int d^{10}x\sqrt{-G}\,e^{-2\phi}\mathcal{R}-\frac{1}{2g_{\scriptscriptstyle 10}^{2}}\int d^{10}x\sqrt{-G}\,e^{-2\phi}{\rm Tr}F^{2}\,.

Comparing the first with the second line in (169), we find:

M108=2(2​π)7​α′4=4​π​Ms8andg102=4α′​M108=4​π​Ms−6.M_{\scriptscriptstyle 10}^{8}=\frac{2}{(2\pi)^{7}\alpha^{\prime 4}}=4\pi M_{s}^{8}\qquad\text{and}\qquad g_{\scriptscriptstyle 10}^{2}=\frac{4}{\alpha^{\prime}M_{\scriptscriptstyle 10}^{8}}=4\pi M_{s}^{-6}\,. (170)

Compactifying on a 6D CY three-fold XX, the 4D Planck scale MPM_{P} turns out to be:

MP2=e−2​⟨ϕ⟩​M108​Vol​(X)=4​π​gs−2​𝒱​Ms2,M_{P}^{2}=e^{-2\langle\phi\rangle}M_{\scriptscriptstyle 10}^{8}{\rm Vol}(X)=4\pi\,g_{s}^{-2}{\cal V}M_{s}^{2}\,, (171)

where we measured the internal volume in units of Ms−1M_{s}^{-1} as Vol⁡(X)=𝒱​ℓs6{\rm Vol}(X)={\cal V}\,\ell_{s}^{6} and we explicitly included factors of the string coupling gs=e⟨ϕ⟩g_{s}=e^{\langle\phi\rangle}. On the other hand, the 4D gauge coupling constant becomes:

αG​U​T−1=4​π​g4−2=4​π​Vol​(X)g102​e2​⟨ϕ⟩=gs−2​𝒱.\alpha_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}^{-1}=4\pi g_{\scriptscriptstyle 4}^{-2}=\frac{4\pi{\rm Vol}(X)}{g_{\scriptscriptstyle 10}^{2}\,e^{2\langle\phi\rangle}}=g_{s}^{-2}{\cal V}\,. (172)

The tree-level expression of the gauge kinetic function f=Sf=S requires Re⁡(S)=g4−2{\rm Re}(S)=g_{4}^{-2}, implying the following normalisation of the definition of the dilaton field:

S=14​π​(e−2​ϕ​𝒱+i​a).S=\frac{1}{4\pi}\left(e^{-2\phi}{\cal V}+{\rm i}\,a\right). (173)

From (172), we immediately realise that there is a tension between large volume and weak coupling for the physical value αG​U​T−1≃25\alpha_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}^{-1}\simeq 25:

𝒱=gs2​αG​U​T−1≃gs2​25≲25forgs≲1.{\cal V}=g_{s}^{2}\alpha_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}^{-1}\simeq g_{s}^{2}25\lesssim 25\qquad\text{for}\qquad g_{s}\lesssim 1\,. (174)

On top of this problem, isotropic compactifications cannot yield the right value of the GUT scale MG​U​T≃2.1⋅1016M_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}\simeq 2.1\cdot 10^{16} GeV which is given by the Kaluza-Klein scale MK​K=Ms/𝒱1/6M_{{\scriptscriptstyle KK}}=M_{s}/{\cal V}^{1/6}. In fact, combining (171) with (172), one finds that the string scale is fixed to be very high:

Ms2=MP24​π​αG​U​T−1≃MP2100​π≃(1.35⋅1017​GeV)2.M_{s}^{2}=\frac{M_{P}^{2}}{4\pi\alpha_{\scriptscriptstyle GUT}^{-1}}\simeq\frac{M_{P}^{2}}{100\pi}\simeq\left(1.35\cdot 10^{17}\,\text{GeV}\right)^{2}\,. (175)

The situation can be improved by focusing on anisotropic compactifications with dd large extra dimensions of size L=x​ℓsL=x\ell_{s} with x≫1x\gg 1 and (6−d)(6-d) small dimensions of string size l=ℓsl=\ell_{s}. The internal volume then becomes Vol⁡(X)=Ld​l(6−d)=xd​ℓs6=𝒱​ℓs6{\rm Vol}(X)=L^{d}l^{(6-d)}=x^{d}\ell_{s}^{6}={\cal V}\,\ell_{s}^{6}, implying that the Kaluza-Klein scale now becomes MK​K=Ms/x=Ms/𝒱1/dM_{\scriptscriptstyle KK}=M_{s}/x=M_{s}/{\cal V}^{1/d}.
